#### **7.5 Genus** *Acropora* **(Family Acroporidae)**

#### **Acroporidae**

Worldwide, *Acropora* are usually among the first corals to show substantial losses in times of stress (Riegl, 2002).

--- SENTENCE 3847 ---
Species of *Acropora* tend to have particularly high vulnerability to predation, disease, sedimentation, and high temperatures (discussed separately below).

--- SENTENCE 3848 ---
Although the earliest fossils of *Acropora* that have been found were from the late Paleocene (54 Ma) and ancestors of 9 of the 20 *Acropora* species groups existed in the Eocene (49–34 Ma), the impressive diversification of the genus *Acropora* is thought to have occurred in the southwestern Pacific very recently, within the past 2 million years (Wallace and Rosen, 2006; Wood, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3849 ---
*Acropora palmata* became a dominant component of western Atlantic reefs about 0.5 Ma.

--- SENTENCE 3850 ---
The Ice Ages have been especially good for the formation of coral reefs, and apparently the diversification of *Acropora*, because of low levels of atmospheric CO2 and because it was a time in which the Mg/Ca ratio of seawater supported the aragonitic mineralogy of coral skeletons (Ries et al., 2006; Stanley, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 3851 ---
During times when environmental conditions are favorable to coral growth, winning in competition for space might have a greater selective advantage than ability to withstand a stressful physical environment.

--- SENTENCE 3852 ---
By the Principle of Allocation (Cody, 1966), phenotypes have to allocate limited resources between competing physiological processes.

--- SENTENCE 3853 ---
If *Acropora* is selected to grow very rapidly to overtop other corals, then it might be cutting costs in complex biochemical defenses against predation, chemicals or infection, such as heat-shock proteins, antioxidants, and innate immunity (Palmer et al., 2010), thereby reducing its ability to resist environmental stresses.

--- SENTENCE 3854 ---
*Acropor*a species became a dominant component of reefs in the later Neogene (23 Ma to present) by their rapid growth, outcompeting for space by growing upward and overtopping.

--- SENTENCE 3855 ---
This rapid growth was achieved by maintaining lower tissue and energetic reserves than slower-growing corals do.

--- SENTENCE 3856 ---
The tissue layer of *Acropora* species is 1.0–1.9 mm thick, while massive corals generally have tissues 2.8–4.0 mm thick (Loya et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3857 ---
The percent nitrogen in the tissues of *Acropora* was found to be 1.55–1.81 while the percent nitrogen in six genera of massive corals was 2.66–4.65 (Rotjan, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 3858 ---
The percent carbon in *Acropora* was 11.74–11.83 while the percent carbon in six genera of massive corals was 19.01–27.59 (Rotjan, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 3859 ---
High energetic reserves help corals withstand or recover from bleaching (Grottoli et al., 2004; Rodrigues and Grottoli, 2007; Rodrigues et al., 2008), so the thin, nutrient-poor tissues of *Acropora* may be a handicap in that regard.

--- SENTENCE 3860 ---
The rates of growth of branching corals, especially *Acropora*, are more directly affected by the physical environment (Gladfelter et al., 1978) while the growth of massive corals is controlled to a greater degree by their own physiology (Smith et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 3861 ---
Similarly, while skeletons of massive corals are usually deposited as dense layers (dissepiments) beneath each polyp, *Acropora* can grow an order of magnitude faster by having an axial polyp deposit a highly porous skeleton.

--- SENTENCE 3862 ---
Acroporids are apparently focused on rapid growth, overtopping, and competition for space, with a cost in resources for withstanding harsh physical environmental factors.

--- SENTENCE 3863 ---
The Pacific Acroporids are a particularly speciose and ecologically important group of corals and, as such, have been the subject of extensive taxonomic, as well as ecological research.

--- SENTENCE 3864 ---
This extensive taxonomic attention has included several authoritative taxonomic revisions, the work of Wallace (1999) providing the best example.

--- SENTENCE 3865 ---
In the course of such revisions, old species names are often subsumed (or renamed), a process known as synonomizing.

--- SENTENCE 3866 ---
Hence, in the future treatment of such species, it will be noted that it is 'synonymous' with additional (generally obsolete) species names.

--- SENTENCE 3867 ---
In these cases, the term synonmy does not indicate current taxonomic uncertainty, rather, it indicates that authoritative taxonomic revision has occurred in the past.

--- SENTENCE 3868 ---
Another manifestation of the special attention given to this speciose group is the recent work of Richards (2009) which has undertaken ecological and genetic comparison of naturally rare and very common species within the *Acropora* genus.

--- SENTENCE 3869 ---
Several useful constructs of Richards' analysis were considered extensively by the BRT in assessing extinction risk among the candidate *Acropora*.

--- SENTENCE 3870 ---
These useful constructions included a ranking of 114 species by geographic range size and a nuanced description of rarity for each species that incorporated global distribution, local distribution (frequency of occurrence at sites within individual localities), and local abundance.

--- SENTENCE 3871 ---
Richards articulates the latter characterization of rarity for each as one of eight Occupancy Types, with Types 1 and 2 representing high risk of global and local extinction, respectively, because of low abundance *combined with* restricted range.

--- SENTENCE 3872 ---
The other six Occupancy Types (3-8) are characterized by some combination of higher abundance and/or greater distribution which yields lower expected extinction risk (Richards, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 3873 ---
These Richards Occupancy Types are listed in the appropriate species' assessments below.

#### **Life History**

*Acropora* are sessile colonies that spawn their gametes into the water column, and the azooxanthellate larvae can survive in the planktonic stage from 4 to 209 days (Graham et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 3874 ---
This has allowed many *Acropora* species to have very wide geographic ranges, both longitudinally and latitudinally (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3875 ---
However, sessile colonies must be within a few meters of each other to have reasonable success in fertilization (Coma and Lasker, 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3876 ---
Vollmer and Palumbi (2007), using DNA sequence data, determined that *Acropora cervicornis* in the Caribbean have limited realized gene flow despite long-distance dispersal potential.

--- SENTENCE 3877 ---
Although spawners with long larval lives can eventually become distributed over broad geographic areas, as is typical for *Acropora*, the year-by-year replenishment of populations requires local source populations.

--- SENTENCE 3878 ---
All species of the genus *Acropora* studied to date are simultaneous hermaphrodites (Baird et al., 2009), with a gametogenic cycle in which eggs develop over a period of about 9 months and testes over about 10 weeks (Babcock et al., 1986; Szmant, 1986; Wallace, 1985).

--- SENTENCE 3879 ---
Fecundity in *Acropora* colonies is generally described as ranging from 3.6 to 15.8 eggs per polyp (Kenyon, 2008; Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3880 ---
Mature eggs of species of *Acropora* are large when compared with those of other corals, ranging from 0.53 to 0.90 mm in mean diameter (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3881 ---
For five *Acropora* species examined by Wallace (1985), the minimum reproductive size ranged from 4 to 7 cm, and the estimated ages ranged from 3 to 5 years.

--- SENTENCE 3882 ---
release gametes as egg-sperm bundles that float to the sea surface, each polyp releasing all its eggs and sperm in one bundle.

--- SENTENCE 3883 ---
Fertilization takes place after the bundles break open at the sea surface.

--- SENTENCE 3884 ---
Sperm concentrations of 106 ml-1 have been found to be optimal for fertilization in the laboratory, and concentrations of this order have been recorded in the field during mass spawning events.

--- SENTENCE 3885 ---
Self-fertilization, although possible, is infrequent.

--- SENTENCE 3886 ---
Gametes remain viable and achieve high fertilization rates for up to 8 hours after spawning (Kenyon, 1994).

--- SENTENCE 3887 ---
Embryogenesis takes place over several hours, and further development leads to a planula that is competent to settle in 4 to 5 days after fertilization.

--- SENTENCE 3888 ---
*Acropora* spp. can show a high degree of hybridization (Kenyon, 1994;

--- SENTENCE 3889 ---
Richards et al., 2008b; Van Oppen et al., 2002; Van Oppen et al., 2000), which can complicate taxonomic classification but allow persistence of the genus if the hybrids are reproductively viable.

--- SENTENCE 3890 ---
As sessile spawners with planktonic larvae, the Critical Risk Threshold assessments for *Acropora* species must weigh the broad distributions that provide replicated opportunities for potential escape from local disturbances against the necessity to have colonies in close enough proximity to have successful fertilization of enough eggs to replenish the attrition of the spawning stock.

--- SENTENCE 3891 ---
If the effective population size (i.e., the number of genotypes [might be substantially less than the number of colonies in highly clonal species] close enough for successful fertilization) becomes too low to replenish the population, then the positive-feedback depensatory processes begin.

--- SENTENCE 3892 ---
It is worth noting that Edinger and Risk (1995) concluded that brooding corals survived the harsh environmental conditions better than did the spawners in the western Atlantic during the major extinctions of the Oligocene-Miocene transition period.

--- SENTENCE 3893 ---
Many *Acropora* have branching morphologies, making them potentially susceptible to fragmentation.

--- SENTENCE 3894 ---
Fragment survival can increase coral abundance in the short-term but does not contribute new genotypes (or evolutionary opportunities) to the population.

#### **Threats**

**Thermal Stress:**

--- SENTENCE 3895 ---
The genus *Acropora* is widely recognized as being particularly prone to expelling their zooxanthellae when the water becomes anomalously warm.

--- SENTENCE 3896 ---
In a series of field assessments, Marshall and Baird (2000) noted that 14 of the 22 species of *Acropora* showed a "severe" response to increased water temperature.

--- SENTENCE 3897 ---
The others were "mixed" and possibly "severe" with them also.

--- SENTENCE 3898 ---
McClanahan et al. (2007) surveyed thousands of corals of 39 genera and found *Acropora* to be among the most sensitive to anomalously warm waters, with only 5 genera ranking higher.

--- SENTENCE 3899 ---
Branching *Acropora* tended to be more severely affected than tabular *Acropora* (Floros et al., 2004; Loya et al., 2001), although this was not always the case (Marshall and Baird, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 3900 ---
In addition, bleaching-induced mortality can be severe; *Acropora* in the southeastern Arabian Gulf suffered > 90% mortality during the 1996 bleaching event (Riegl, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3901 ---
However, remnants of *Acropora vaughani* deep inside the reef framework survived after the 1998 mass bleaching event (Riegl and Piller, 2001), providing for potentially accelerated recovery.

--- SENTENCE 3902 ---
A modeling study by Riegl and Purkis (2009) emphasized the importance of larval connectivity in promoting recovery of coral populations following repeated bleaching events and predicted that mass bleaching mortality events must remain infrequent (< 15 years) to avoid *Acropora* spp.

--- SENTENCE 3903 ---
collapse in Arabian Gulf reef communities.

--- SENTENCE 3904 ---
Even if bleaching is only temporary, physiological stress and the decrease in nutrition are likely to have the synergistic effects of lowered fecundity and increased susceptibility to disease (Bruno et al., 2007; Muller et al., 2008; Whelan et al., 2007).

--- SENTENCE 3905 ---
Fertilization and larval stages of *Acropora* spp. have also been shown to be particularly vulnerable to anomalously warm temperatures, displaying reduced fertilization, developmental abnormalities and reduced larval survivorship (Negri et al., 2007; Randall and Szmant, 2009a).

--- SENTENCE 3906 ---
**Acidification**: Acidification can have a variety of effects on *Acropora.*

--- SENTENCE 3907 ---
While increased CO2 (increased acidity) does not appear to affect the survival of *Acropora* larvae, fertilization, settlement, rate of zooxanthellae acquisition, and postsettlement growth are all significantly impaired (Albright et al., 2010; Suwa et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 3908 ---
Elevated CO2 also induces bleaching in *Acropora*, even more so than temperature increases (Anthony et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 3909 ---
CO2 enrichment to 600–790 ppm enhanced maximum photosynthetic rates in *Acropora formosa* (Crawley et al., 2010), but elevated CO2 levels had no effect on photosynthesis or respiration in *Acropora eurystoma*

--- SENTENCE 3910 ---
(Schneider and Erez, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 3911 ---
Moderate increases in CO2 may enhance *Acropora* productivity, which falls back to zero at high CO2 (Anthony et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 3912 ---
More consistently, elevated CO2 tends to decrease *Acropora* growth and calcification rates (Anthony et al., 2008;

--- SENTENCE 3913 ---
Gattuso et al., 1998; Renegar and Riegl, 2005; Schneider and Erez, 2006), primarily as a result of carbonate ion concentration rather than pH or total inorganic carbon levels (Schneider and Erez, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 3914 ---
Although other coral taxa may experience a similar overall reduction in calcification based on CO2, *Acropora* show a greater reduction in the mineral density of its skeletal crystals (Marubini et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 3915 ---
Decadal-scale reductions in growth rates of the Caribbean congener, *Acropora palmata*, in Curaçao have been attributed to acidification (Bak et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 3916 ---
**Disease**: *Acropora* are vulnerable to most of the diseases known to affect scleractinian corals and are more commonly affected by acute and lethal conditions (e.g., "white diseases") than some other taxa.

--- SENTENCE 3917 ---
The greatest losses of corals to diseases throughout the western Atlantic have been *Acropora palmata* and *Acropora cervicornis* (Aronson and Precht, 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3918 ---
By drastically reducing the population fecundity, the depensatory effects of disease mortality can act synergistically with the depensatory effects of low colony density impairing successful fertilization, with both factors operating by positive feedback.

--- SENTENCE 3919 ---
As an example from Eastern Dry Rocks Reef in the Florida Keys: "During the 7 years of the photostation survey, living cover of *Acropora palmata* decreased by 98% [from white pox].

--- SENTENCE 3920 ---
Coral recruitment was not observed within the photostation during the 7-year survey (Patterson et al., 2002).

--- SENTENCE 3921 ---
Other examples of diseases impacting *Acropora* include: black-band disease in Australia (Miller, 1996), skeleton-eroding band disease in Jordan (Winkler et al., 2004), a fungal disease in Kenya (McClanahan et al., 2004b), a yellow-band disease in the Arabian Gulf (Korrubel and Riegl, 1998; Riegl, 2002), and white-band disease in Saudi Arabia (Antonius, 1985).

--- SENTENCE 3922 ---
**Predation:** *Acropora* species are preferred prey of most corallivorous invertebrate predators, e.g., *Acanthaster planci*, *Drupella* spp., *Quoyula monodonta*, *Coralliophila abbreviata*, and *Hermodice carunculata*.

--- SENTENCE 3923 ---
Of 14 species of corallivorous butterflyfishes on the Great Barrier Reef, 11 preferred *Acropor*a and at least one chaetodontid fed exclusively on *Acropora*

--- SENTENCE 3924 ---
Of 14 species of corallivorous butterflyfishes on the Great Barrier Reef, 11 preferred *Acropor*a and at least one chaetodontid fed exclusively on *Acropora*

--- SENTENCE 3925 ---
Chaetodontids with territories consume between 400 and 700 bites per hour from tabular *Acropora* (Gochfeld, 2004; Tricas, 1985) and corallivorous chaetodontids can occur at average densities of 50–70 fish per 1000 m2 .

--- SENTENCE 3926 ---
This intense predation appears to have been sustainable under the environmental conditions of the Pleistocene (2.6 M to 12,000 years ago) that were favorable to the growth of *Acropora* colonies.

--- SENTENCE 3927 ---
In view of the relatively low nitrogen and carbon in the tissue of *Acropora* in combination with its preference as prey by such a disparate group of corallivores, it is reasonable to assume that *Acropora* species do not invest a major portion of metabolic energy in biochemical or structural defenses against predation.

--- SENTENCE 3928 ---
Their defense against both competitors and predators appears to be rapid growth.

--- SENTENCE 3929 ---
However, it has been shown that when a living coral population is substantially reduced by natural or anthropogenic disturbances to below a threshold (< 5% cover), the risk of overpredation produces a positive-feedback depensatory effect (Jayewardene et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 3930 ---
Even with the rates of predation staying the same as in the stable reef community, once a severe disturbance lowers the living coral cover below a threshold, predation by corallivorous invertebrates (Glynn, 1985a; 1990; Knowlton et al., 1990) or fishes (Guzmán and Robertson, 1989; McClanahan et al., 2005b; Rotjan et al., 2006) can seriously impede or even prevent the recovery of the coral populations.

--- SENTENCE 3931 ---
The depensatory effects of predation can act synergistically with the depensatory effects of colonies being too spread out for successful fertilization.

--- SENTENCE 3932 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):**

--- SENTENCE 3933 ---
In clear water, *Acropora* colonies of a number of species have been reported to be living apparently well at 60-m depth and deeper (Bare et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 3934 ---
But *Acropora* colonies can be restricted by turbid waters.

--- SENTENCE 3935 ---
Experiments by Rogers (1979) showed *Acropora* to be the most sensitive to shading (a proxy for turbidity) of the genera she tested.

--- SENTENCE 3936 ---
In two communities composed of a total of 159 species of stony corals that extended from forereef slopes into turbid bays up to the mouths of rivers in Guam, colonies of *Acropora* were among the first to drop out (Randall and Birkeland, 1978).

--- SENTENCE 3937 ---
Certain *Acropora* growth forms are effective at passive sediment rejection (Stafford-Smith and Ormond, 1992)—for example, cylindrical branching or perforated tabular forms.

--- SENTENCE 3938 ---
However, the cylindrical form of branching *Acropora* and the perforated form of tabular *Acropora* possibly reduce the vulnerability of adult colonies to sediment per se, but *Acropora* are not particularly adept at actively removing sediment (Hubbard and Pocock, 1972), and Rogers (1983) found *Acropora* to be most vulnerable of the genera she studied.

--- SENTENCE 3939 ---
As with most corals, adult colonies of *Acropora* have been reported to be especially affected by sedimentation during reproduction.

--- SENTENCE 3940 ---
Turbidity and coating by sediment decrease the metabolic energy available to corals by reducing the light available for photosynthesis by the zooxanthellae and increasing energy needed for the removal of sediment by the coral animal through mucus production and ciliary action.

--- SENTENCE 3941 ---
These decreases in metabolic energy reduce the fecundity of the coral (Tomascik and Sander, 1987b).

--- SENTENCE 3942 ---
Lateritic soils are typical of tropical islands.

--- SENTENCE 3943 ---
The iron in lateritic ("red") soils and other chemicals in runoff interfere with synchronization among colonies, egg-sperm recognition and interactions, fertilization, and embryological development (Richmond et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 3944 ---
Sediment, toxins, and elevated nutrients all reduce fertilization success, survival, and settlement of *Acropora* larvae (Gilmour, 1999;

--- SENTENCE 3945 ---
Humphrey et al., 2008; Reichelt-Brushett and Harrison, 2000; Ward and Harrison, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 3946 ---
The recruitment of larvae is inhibited by sediment covering signals for substratum recognition, covering the appropriate hard surface, and burying the newly settled corals if they are temporarily given the chance to settle.

--- SENTENCE 3947 ---
Sediment particles, specifically lateritic red clay and mud particles, serve as nuclei for bacterial and microfaunal aggregations in organically rich materials that settle on the reef substrata and contribute to the biological oxygen demand on reef surfaces at night (Richmond et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 3948 ---
By reducing success in fecundity, fertilization, larval settlement, and survival of juveniles, sedimentation and associated turbidity have depensatory effects (Birrell et al., 2005).

#### **Collection/Trade**

As a whole, *Acropora* are heavily traded (Table 7.5.1).

--- SENTENCE 3949 ---
However, trade quotas or reported exports are generally listed only at the genus level, making assessment of species-level threat difficult.

--- SENTENCE 3950 ---
Export records are available for *Acropora striata*, *Acropora tenella*, and *Acropora vaughani*.

#### **7.5.1** *Acropora aculeus* **Dana, 1846**

!

--- SENTENCE 3971 ---
*Acropora aculeus* photos from Veron (2000).

--- SENTENCE 3972 ---
#### **Characteristics**

*Acropora aculeus* forms flattened corymbose colonies to about 40 cm in diameter (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3973 ---
It is typically flattopped, clumping, or tabular, with colonies formed by horizontal branches that protrude short slender vertical branches.

--- SENTENCE 3974 ---
Colonies are usually a pale grey-green in color but can be bright blue-green or yellow.

--- SENTENCE 3975 ---
The tips of the branches can be yellow, lime-green, pale blue or brown (Veron, 2000).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None, but *Acropora aculeus* can be confused with *Acropora latistella,* which also has a broad depth and geographic range.

--- SENTENCE 3976 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: No fossil records of *Acropora aculeus* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

#### **Global Distribution**

*Acropora aculeus* has a relatively broad range, having the 15th largest range of 114 *Acropora* species examined (Richards, 2009), extending from east Africa, the Comorros, and Seychelles in the Indian Ocean all the way to Pitcairn Island in the southeastern Pacific Ocean.

--- SENTENCE 3977 ---
Latitudinally, it has been reported from Japanese waters in the northern hemisphere across the southern Great Barrier Reef and Mozambique in the southern hemisphere.

!

--- SENTENCE 3978 ---
*Acropora aculeus* distribution from IUCN copied from http://www.iucnredlist.org.

!

--- SENTENCE 3979 ---
*Acropora aculeus* distribution from Wallace (1999).

--- SENTENCE 3980 ---
The black squares are specimen-based records in *Acropora* database at the Museum of Tropical Queensland, the stars are type localities of senior and junior synonyms, and the black triangles are taken from records in the literature.

--- SENTENCE 3981 ---
When the triangles are open (not black), the records from the literature are possibly misidentifications.

!

--- SENTENCE 3982 ---
*Acropora aculeus* distribution from Veron (2002).

#### **U.S. Distribution**

According to both the IUCN Species Account and the CITES species database, *Acropora aculeus* occurs in American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the U.S. minor outlying islands.

--- SENTENCE 3983 ---
A search of published and unpublished records of occurrence in U.S. waters indicates *Acropora aculeus* has been reported from Tutuila and Ofu-Olosega in American Samoa (Birkeland, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 3984 ---
data; Lamberts, 1983; Lovell and McLardy, 2008; Mundy, 1996; National Park Service, 2009), Guam (Burdick, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 3985 ---
data; Randall, 2003; Wallace, 1999), Palmyra Atoll (Williams et al., 2008b), Kingman Reef, and Wake Atoll (CRED, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 3986 ---
Within federally protected waters, *Acropora aculeus* has been recorded from the following areas (Kenyon et al., 2010b):

- Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument (Palmyra, Kingman, Wake)
- National Park of American Samoa, Ofu Island unit

#### **Habitat**

*Acropora aculeus* has a broad depth range.

--- SENTENCE 3987 ---
It is particularly abundant in shallow lagoons and is common in most habitats where it is protected from direct wave action.

--- SENTENCE 3988 ---
**Depth range**: *Acropora aculeus* has been reported in water depths ranging from low tide to at least 20 m (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3989 ---
#### **Abundance**

Abundance of *Acropora aculeus* has been reported as generally common and locally abundant, especially in the central Indo-Pacific (Veron, 2000).

####

--- SENTENCE 3990 ---
**Life History**

*Acropora aculeus* is a hermaphroditic spawner that is a participant in mass broadcast spawning in some localities (Babcock et al., 1986; Babcock et al., 1994).

--- SENTENCE 3991 ---
Growth is determinate or sometimes semideterminate (Wallace, 1985).

--- SENTENCE 3992 ---
For more genus level information, see Section 7.5: Genus *Acropora*.

#### **Threats**

For each of these possible threats, see also Section 7.5:

--- SENTENCE 3993 ---
Genus *Acropora* for additional genus level information.

--- SENTENCE 3994 ---
The genus *Acropora* is consistently ranked among the coral genera most severely susceptible to bleaching (Marshall and Baird, 2000; McClanahan et al., 2007; McClanahan et al., 2005a), although the genus may have differential responses across regions during mass bleaching mortalities (McClanahan et al., 2004a).

--- SENTENCE 3995 ---
*Acropora aculeus* tolerates high temperatures in back-reef pools in Ofu, American Samoa (Craig et al., 2001), although it is not abundant and acroporids still bleach in these pools (Fenner and Heron, 2008).

--- SENTENCE 3996 ---
Most acroporids in the Great Barrier Reef host clade C zooxanthellae, but *Acropora aculeus* hosts clade D (LaJeunesse et al., 2004a) as well as clade C (Van Oppen et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3997 ---
As *Acropora aculeus* bleaches via loss of zooxanthellae (Hoegh-Guldberg, 1994) and corals preferentially expel clade C during bleaching (Rowan et al., 1997), the presence of clade D could either confer bleaching resistance or simply indicate stressful conditions.

--- SENTENCE 3998 ---
In any case, *Acropora aculeus* has moderately high bleaching susceptibility relative to other acroporids on the Great Barrier Reef (Done et al., 2003) and, as a whole, bleaching presents a high risk to this species.

--- SENTENCE 3999 ---
No specific research has addressed the effects of acidification on *Acropora aculeus,* but experiments on acidification impacts have demonstrated negative effects on *Acropora* calcification (Anthony et al., 2008;

--- SENTENCE 4000 ---
Marubini et al., 2003; Renegar and Riegl, 2005; Schneider and Erez, 2006) and productivity (Anthony et al., 2008; Crawley et al., 2010), as well as impaired fertilization and settlement success in *Acropora palmata* (Albright et al., 2010) and reduced growth and zooxanthellae uptake in juveniles (Suwa et al., 2010)*.*

--- SENTENCE 4001 ---
In general, most corals studied have shown negative relationships between acidification and growth (Table 3.2.2), and acidification is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007, Silverman et al. 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4002 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have already caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 4003 ---
**Disease:** Susceptibility and impacts of disease on *Acropora aculeus* are not known, although in general *Acropora* species are moderately to highly susceptible to disease.

--- SENTENCE 4004 ---
Additionally, ample evidence show that diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species (Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009), and there is evidence that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Sutherland et al., 2004, Green and Bruckner 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4005 ---
**Predation (COTS, snails, other):** Most *Acropora* are preferentially consumed by crown-of-thorns seastars, *Acanthaster planci* (Colgan, 1987) and by corallivorous snails (B. Vargas-Ángel, CRED, Honolulu, HI, pers.

--- SENTENCE 4006 ---
When predation occurs, it can have significant effects—corymbose corals (including *Acropora aculeus*) with lesions from *Drupella* predation suffer 33%–54% mortality within 3 months (Cumming, 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4007 ---
Predation may, therefore, present a moderate risk at local scales but would be unlikely to lead to extinction.

--- SENTENCE 4008 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):**

--- SENTENCE 4009 ---
The specific effects of LBSP stresses are largely unknown for *Acropora aculeus*.

--- SENTENCE 4010 ---
LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually,and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 4011 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 4012 ---
As a whole, the genus *Acropora* has been heavily involved in international trade with 50,000– 270,000 reported exported pieces per year from Indonesia (CITES, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4013 ---
As the species in this genus can be difficult to distinguish by nonexperts, it is possible that *Acropora aculeus* could be affected.

#### **Risk Assessment**

!

--- SENTENCE 4014 ---
Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Acropora aculeus* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 4015 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora aculeus* include the relatively high susceptibility of the genus *Acropora* to common threats (bleaching, acidification, disease, predation, and pollution).

--- SENTENCE 4016 ---
The high bleaching rate of acroporid corals is the primary known threat of extinction for *Acropora aculeus*.

--- SENTENCE 4017 ---
Factors that reduce potential extinction risk (decrease the likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) include the very wide geographic range, the broad depth range, the fact that it is often common and sometimes abundant, and the somewhat broad range of suitable habitats for *Acropora aculeus*.

--- SENTENCE 4018 ---
Vulnerability of *Acropora aculeus* may be somewhat ameliorated by the fact that it is known to occur in deeper water than many other acroporids and perhaps experiences disturbances (e.g. bleaching, storms, etc.)

--- SENTENCE 4019 ---
These characteristics tend toward species persistence (Richards, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4020 ---
The overall likelihood that *Acropora aculeus* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be in the "less likely than not" risk category with a mean likelihood of 49% and a standard error (SE) of 12% (Fig.

This SE was calculated by taking the standard deviation of the seven mean voting scores of the BRT members and shows the coherence among the BRT.

The uncertainty of the BRT is reflected in the range of votes of 10%–90% (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 4023 ---
and the average range of likelihood estimates of the seven BRT voters (51%).

--- SENTENCE 4024 ---
The overall wide range of votes reflects the uncertainty among BRT members inherent in the lack of adequate ecological and demographic information for *Acropora aculeus*.

#### **7.5.2** *Acropora acuminata* **Verrill, 1864**

!

--- SENTENCE 4025 ---
*Acropora acuminata* photo and coralite plan from Veron (2000).

--- SENTENCE 4026 ---
#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora acuminata* typically form a tabular base of fused horizontal branches that turn upward and taper to points.

--- SENTENCE 4027 ---
Colonies are most often pale or bright brown or blue.

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 4028 ---
*Acropora acuminata* was originally called *Madrepora nigra*, probably because drying specimens turn black (Wallace, 1999; Wells, 1954).

--- SENTENCE 4029 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: No fossil records of *Acropora acuminata* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

#### **Global Distribution**

*Acropora acuminata* has a very broad range, having the fifth most extensive range of 114 *Acropora* species examined (Richards, 2009), extending longitudinally from the Red Sea all the way to Pitcairn Island in the southeastern Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 4030 ---
Its total range covers 110 million km2 .

--- SENTENCE 4031 ---
It extends latitudinally from Taiwan in the northern hemisphere across the Great Barrier Reef in the southern hemisphere.

--- SENTENCE 4032 ---
It can be very common in the center of its range (e.g., Indonesia), but it can be uncommon in the outer parts of its range (Wallace, 1999).

!

data; Randall, 2003), Howland and Baker Islands, Kingman Reef, Wake Atoll (CRED, unpubl.

- Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary, Tutuila

**Depth range**: *Acropora acuminata* is not well known, although it has been reported in waters ranging from 15 to 20 m (IUCN, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4043 ---
#### **Abundance**

####

--- SENTENCE 4044 ---
**Life History**

Like most of its congeners, *Acropora acuminata* is a broadcast spawner (Baird et al., 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4045 ---
However, it may achieve some degree of reproductive isolation in some locations by not spawning synchronously with the majority of its congeners (Baird et al., 2010; Carroll et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 4046 ---
Growth is determinate (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4047 ---
For more genus level information, see Section 7.5: Genus *Acropora*.

--- SENTENCE 4050 ---

#### **7.5.3** *Acropora aspera* **Dana, 1846**

!

--- SENTENCE 4080 ---
*Acropora aspera* photos copied from (*color*) Veron (2000) and (*black and white*) corallite plan from Wallace (1999).

--- SENTENCE 4081 ---
#### **Characteristics**

*Acropora aspera* typically forms arborescent to caespitose-corymbose clumps of thick, relatively stout branches.

--- SENTENCE 4082 ---
The thickness and stoutness of the branches can vary considerably, depending on their exposure to wave energy.

--- SENTENCE 4083 ---
Taller colonies can be found in shallow protected habitats.

--- SENTENCE 4084 ---
Branches tend to be of relatively even length.

--- SENTENCE 4085 ---
The low, sprawling colonies can appear corymbose because of the even length of the branches or height of the colonies (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4086 ---
The clumps can sometimes be extensive, forming large uninterrupted stands.

--- SENTENCE 4087 ---
On exposed forereefs, *Acropora aspera* colonies can be caespitose-corymbose with stout, tapering, highly anastomosed branches and short, thick secondary branches with crowded radial corallites of relatively uniform size (see upper black and white photograph above; Wallace 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4088 ---
In shallow protected waters, *Acropora aspera* can form micro-atolls.

--- SENTENCE 4089 ---
In deeper protected waters, *Acropora aspera* can form arborescent colonies with sturdy branches that seldom anastomose.

--- SENTENCE 4090 ---
In protected waters, the radial corallites are less crowded than in exposed habitats.

--- SENTENCE 4091 ---
In areas of reduced light (e.g., shallow, turbid lagoons or deeper reef slopes), the branches are relatively thin and the corallites are relatively small and widely spaced (see lower black and white photograph above; Wallace 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4092 ---
*Acropora aspera* colonies are pale brown, beige, or pale blue-grey, green or cream (Randall and Myers, 1983).

####

--- SENTENCE 4093 ---
**Taxonomy**

Taxonomic issues: None.

--- SENTENCE 4094 ---
**Family:** Acroporidae

**Evolutionary and geologic history**: Fossil records of *Acropora aspera* have been reportedly found from the Pleistocene (1.8–0.01 Ma; Wallace, 1999).

#### **Global Distribution**

*Acropora aspera* has a relatively broad range, having the 46th largest range of 114 *Acropora* species examined (Richards, 2009), extending longitudinally from the Red Sea (Antonius et al., 1990) and Oman (Wallace, 1999) to Samoa (eastcentral Pacific Ocean).

--- SENTENCE 4095 ---
It extends latitudinally from Japanese waters in the northern hemisphere across the Great Barrier Reef in the southern hemisphere.

#### **U.S. Distribution**

According to both the IUCN Species Account and the CITES species database, *Acropora aspera* occurs in American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the U.S. minor outlying islands.

--- SENTENCE 4098 ---

--- SENTENCE 4099 ---
data; Lamberts, 1983; Mundy, 1996), Guam (Amesbury et al., 1999; Burdick, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 4100 ---
data; Randall, 2003; Wallace, 1999), Palmyra Atoll (Williams et al., 2008b), and Kingman Reef (CRED, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 4101 ---
- Within federally protected waters, *Acropora aspera* has been recorded from the following areas (Kenyon et al., 2010b):
- Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument (Palmyra, Kingman)
- National Park of American Samoa, Ofu Island unit
- Rose Atoll Marine National Monument
- War in the Pacific National Historical Park, Guam

#### **Habitat**

**Habitat**: *Acropora aspera* has been reported to occupy a broad range of habitats and its colony structure varies substantially with habitat (Wallace, 1999), as described above in "Characteristics.

--- SENTENCE 4102 ---
"

**Depth range**: *Acropora aspera* has been reported in water depths ranging from low tide to at least 10 m (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4103 ---
#### **Abundance**

Abundance of *Acropora aspera* has been reported as sometimes locally common (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4104 ---
*Acropora aspera* can occasionally live in extensive clumps with dimensions of several meters.

#### **Life History**

*Acropora aspera* is a hermaphroditic spawner (Babcock et al., 1994; Simpson, 1985).

--- SENTENCE 4105 ---
While it is a participant in mass broadcast spawning in some localities, asynchronyous gamete development on the Great Barrier Reef (Baird and Marshall, 2002) and New Caledonia (Baird et al., 2010) may provide a degree of reproductive isolation, although *Acropora aspera* has been shown to hybridize with other acroporids (Van Oppen et al., 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4106 ---
Gamete development in *Acropora aspera* may be aborted in years with storm impacts (Bothwell, 1981).

--- SENTENCE 4107 ---
Asexual reproduction can account for the majority of *Acropora aspera* population structure in certain areas and can lead to local dominance (Birkeland et al., 1979; Bothwell, 1981; Highsmith, 1982).

--- SENTENCE 4108 ---
As noted above, *Acropora aspera* has multiple growth forms.

--- SENTENCE 4109 ---
Growth varies with the influence of monsoon season, and skeletal extension, accretion, and density are all influenced by wave energy (Brown et al., 1985).

--- SENTENCE 4110 ---
*Acropora aspera* has been utilized for a range of laboratory studies, including nitrogen metabolism (Crossland and Barnes, 1974; 1977; Streamer, 1980), calcification (Barnes, 1982; Barnes and Crossland, 1982; Crossland and Barnes, 1974), and lipid metabolism (Crossland et al., 1980).

--- SENTENCE 4111 ---
For more genus level information, see Section 7.5: Genus *Acropora*.

#### **Threats**

For each of these possible threats, see also Section 7.5:

--- SENTENCE 4112 ---
Genus *Acropora* for additional genus level information.

--- SENTENCE 4113 ---
*Acropora* are consistently ranked among the coral genera most severely susceptible to bleaching (Marshall and Baird, 2000; McClanahan et al., 2007; McClanahan et al., 2005a), although the genus may have differential responses across regions during mass bleaching mortalities (McClanahan et al., 2004a).

--- SENTENCE 4114 ---
*Acropora aspera* is among the most bleaching-susceptible of the acroporids on the Great Barrier Reef (Done et al., 2003), where it harbors primarily clade C2 zooxanthellae (Van Oppen et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 4115 ---
It suffered 65% mortality in Fiji during the 2000 event (Cumming et al., 2002), but was one of the few species in good condition in Okinawa 5–10 months after the 1998 event (Stimson et al., 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4116 ---
The species can also suffer substantial mortality during cold-water bleaching events (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2005).

--- SENTENCE 4117 ---
*Acropora aspera* contains green fluorescent proteins, but elevated temperatures reduce their effectiveness in this species, making it hypersensitive to bleaching (Dove, 2004).

--- SENTENCE 4118 ---
Other researchers have found that thermal history enhances photoprotection and reduces bleaching in *Acropora aspera* (Middlebrook et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 4119 ---
However, when it bleaches, *Acropora aspera* can experience reduced fecundity (Ward et al., 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4120 ---
Although range expansion was not directly considered in this analysis, corals in the *Acropora aspera* group had a broader range in Australia during the Pleistocene than today and are predicted to potentially expand southward as temperatures increase (Greenstein and Pandolfi, 2008).

--- SENTENCE 4121 ---
No specific research has addressed the effects of acidification on *Acropora aspera,* but experiments on acidification impacts have demonstrated negative effects on *Acropora* calcification (Anthony et al., 2008;

--- SENTENCE 4122 ---
Marubini et al., 2003; Renegar and Riegl, 2005; Schneider and Erez, 2006) and productivity (Anthony et al., 2008; Crawley et al., 2010), as well as impaired fertilization and settlement success in *Acropora palmata* (Albright et al., 2010) and reduced growth and zooxanthellae uptake in juveniles (Suwa et al., 2010), In general, most corals studied have shown negative relationships between acidification and growth (Table 3.2.2), and acidification is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007, Silverman et al. 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4123 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have already caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 4124 ---
**Disease:** Susceptibility and impacts of disease on *Acropora aspera* are not known, although in general *Acropora* species are moderately to highly susceptible to disease.

--- SENTENCE 4125 ---
*Acropora aspera* experiences subacute black-band disease (UNEP, 2010), as well as ciliate infections (Antonius and Lipscomb, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4126 ---
The ecological and population impacts of disease have not been established for this species.

--- SENTENCE 4127 ---
Bacterial communities on the surface of *Acropora aspera* also change as a result of bleaching, which potentially makes it more susceptible to disease (Ainsworth and Hoegh-Guldberg, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4128 ---
Most *Acropora* are preferentially consumed by crown-of-thorns seastars, *Acanthaster planci* (Colgan, 1987) and by corallivorous snails (B. Vargas-Ángel, CRED, Honolulu, HI, pers.

--- SENTENCE 4129 ---
*Acropora aspera* is a preferred prey of *Acanthaster planci* (Sonoda and Paul, 1993) and, when killed, is rapidly overgrown by algae (Belk and Belk, 1975).

--- SENTENCE 4130 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):** Toxins and nutrients have been reported to have deleterious effects on *Acropora aspera*.

--- SENTENCE 4131 ---
Cyanide (used for fish collection in some areas) significantly reduced the photosynthetic performance and induced bleaching in *Acropora aspera* (Jones and Hoegh-Guldberg, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4132 ---
Although there was temporal variability, *Acropora aspera* produced smaller, fewer eggs and had reduced testes development when exposed to nitrogen, while phosphorus produced fewer but larger eggs (Ward and Harrison, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4133 ---
*Acropora aspera* appears to have mixed susceptibility to runoff.

--- SENTENCE 4134 ---
The species was found to be relatively tolerant of silty/turbid water in the South China Sea (Latypov and Dautova, 2005), but suffered complete mortality when exposed to hyposaline waters during a 1991 flood in the Keppel Islands, Australia (Van Woesik, 1991).

LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 4135 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 4136 ---
As a whole, the genus *Acropora* has been heavily involved in international trade with 50,000– 270,000 reported exported pieces per year from Indonesia (CITES, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4137 ---
As the species in this genus can be difficult to distinguish by nonexperts, it is possible that *Acropora aspera* could be affected.

--- SENTENCE 4139 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora aspera* include the relatively high susceptibility of the genus *Acropora* to common threats (bleaching, acidification, disease, predation, and pollution).

--- SENTENCE 4140 ---
The high bleaching rate of acroporid corals is the primary known threat of extinction for *Acropora aspera*.

--- SENTENCE 4141 ---
Factors that reduce the potential extinction risk (decrease likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora aspera* are the wide geographic range, it is often common and sometimes abundant, and the somewhat broad range of habitats that *Acropora aspera* finds acceptable, including its ability to grow in a variety of morphologies that are conditioned to the habitat characteristics.

--- SENTENCE 4142 ---
These characteristics tend toward species persistence.

#### **7.5.4** *Acropora dendrum* **Bassett-Smith, 1890**

!

--- SENTENCE 4148 ---
*Acropora dendrum* photos and corallite plan from Veron (2000).

--- SENTENCE 4149 ---
#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora dendrum* are usually 0.5–1 m across and are corymbose plates with widely-spaced, tapering branchlets.

--- SENTENCE 4150 ---
Their axial corallites are small.

--- SENTENCE 4151 ---
Radial corallites are immersed or nearly so, giving branchlets a smooth appearance.

--- SENTENCE 4152 ---
Colonies are pale brown or cream in color (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4153 ---
Maximum colony size is 100 cm.

--- SENTENCE 4154 ---
Determinate growth.

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 4155 ---
*Acropora dendrum* is most similar to *Heteropora appressa* and *Acropora microclados*.

--- SENTENCE 4156 ---
Wallace (1999) reported that *Acropora dendrum* is "poorly characterized and may indeed be a 'phantom' species, being made up from specimens that cannot be allocated to other species."

--- SENTENCE 4157 ---
However, the BRT treats it as a nominal species (for taxonomic discussion see Section 2.1.2).

--- SENTENCE 4158 ---
There is no location recorded where it is common or even more abundant than a rare species Wallace (1999).

--- SENTENCE 4159 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: No fossil records of *Acropora dendrum* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

#### **Global Distribution**

The IUCN Red List reports *Acropora dendrum* from the northern Indian Ocean, the central Indo-Pacific, east and west coasts of Australia, Southeast Asia, Japan and the East China Sea.

--- SENTENCE 4160 ---
Other reports are from the oceanic west Pacific and Palau (Randall, 1995) and Vanuatu, Tonga, and Samoa (IUCN, 2010).

According to the IUCN Species Account, *Acropora dendrum* occurs in American Samoa, but no supporting reference is given.

--- SENTENCE 4164 ---

--- SENTENCE 4167 ---
One colony had sub-immersed radial corallites at the bases of branches with reduced cochlearform or labellate radial corallites on the upper parts of branches.

--- SENTENCE 4168 ---
The axial corallites looked fairly large, perhaps 3 mm diameter.

--- SENTENCE 4169 ---
Branches appeared to be about 4–7 mm diameter.

--- SENTENCE 4170 ---
In the other colony, branches appeared to be a bit thinner, and more of the radial corallites appeared to be lying flat against each other.

--- SENTENCE 4171 ---
The axial corallites in the first colony appeared about 1 mm larger than the description of the species by Wallace (1999), but otherwise the photos appear to be a fairly good match.

--- SENTENCE 4172 ---
*Acropora dendrum* was not observed elsewhere in American Samoa by Fenner during dedicated surveys conducted at 38 sites off Ofu-Olosega, Tau, Rose Atoll, Swains, and South Bank in March 2010 (CRED, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 4173 ---
The occurrence of *Acropora dendrum* in American Samoa remains uncertain.

--- SENTENCE 4174 ---
No other published or unpublished data sources indicate the occurrence of *Acropora dendrum* elsewhere in U.S. waters.

#### **Habitat**

**Habitat**: *Acropora dendrum* has been reported to occupy upper reef slopes (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4175 ---
**Depth range**: *Acropora dendrum* has been reported in water depths ranging from 5 m to 20 m (Carpenter et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 4176 ---
#### **Abundance**

Abundance of *Acropora dendrum* has been reported as uncommon or rare (Veron, 2000; Veron and Wallace, 1984).

--- SENTENCE 4177 ---

*Acropora dendrum* is a hermaphroditic spawner (Mezaki et al., 2007; Wallace, 1985) with lecithotrophic larvae (Baird et al., 2009).

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora donei* are table-like, up to 2 m in diameter, and consist of masses of fused horizontal branches.

--- SENTENCE 4203 ---
Their peripheral branches are all horizontal; those towards the colony center have upturned ends.

--- SENTENCE 4204 ---
All branches have blunt ends and are neatly arranged.

--- SENTENCE 4205 ---
Radial corallites are usually in two sizes, the larger of which have flaring lips.

--- SENTENCE 4206 ---
The coenosteum is coarse, giving a rough appearance to branches.

--- SENTENCE 4207 ---
Colonies are green, white, cream, rarely pale brown in color (Veron, 2000).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.*Acropora donei* is similar to *Acropora yongei*, which has similar corallites but does not have upturned branches.

--- SENTENCE 4208 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: No fossil records of *Acropora donei* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4209 ---
has a relatively broad range overall, having the 44th largest range of 114 *Acropora* species examined (Richards, 2009).

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora globiceps* are digitate and usually small.

--- SENTENCE 4247 ---
The size and appearance of branches depend on degree of exposure to wave action but are always short and closely compacted.

--- SENTENCE 4248 ---
Colonies exposed to strong wave action have pyramid-shaped branchlets.

--- SENTENCE 4249 ---
Corallites are irregular in size, those on colonies on reef slopes are tubular, and those on reef flat colonies are more immersed.

--- SENTENCE 4250 ---
Axial corallites are small and sometimes indistinguishable.

--- SENTENCE 4251 ---
Radial corallites are irregular in size and are sometimes arranged in rows down the sides of branches.

--- SENTENCE 4252 ---
Colonies are uniform blue (which may photograph purple) or cream in color (Veron, 2000).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 4253 ---
*Acropora globiceps* is similar to *Acropora gemmifera*, which has radial corallites increasing in size down the sides of branches.

--- SENTENCE 4254 ---
Colonies exposed to strong wave action have a growth-form similar to that of *Acropora monticulosa*.

--- SENTENCE 4255 ---
Corallites are similar to those of *Acropora secale* and *Acropora retusa* (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4256 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: Fossil records of *Acropora globiceps* have been reported from the Pleistocene (0.01–1.8 Ma) from Niue (Wallace, 1999).

####

--- SENTENCE 4257 ---

*Acropora globiceps* has been reported from the central Indo-Pacific, the oceanic west Pacific, and the central Pacific (IUCN, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4259 ---
comm., April 2010, not shown on maps), the Philippines, Andaman Islands, Polynesia, and Micronesia (IUCN, 2010) and Pitcairn (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4260 ---
It has been reported as common and relatively widespread longitudinally but restricted latitudinally and has a narrow depth range.

--- SENTENCE 4261 ---
*Acropora globiceps* has the 88th largest (26th smallest) range of 114 *Acropora* species examined (Richards, 2009).

Marubini et al., 2003; Renegar and Riegl, 2005; Schneider and Erez, 2006) and productivity (Anthony et al., 2008; Crawley et al., 2010), as well as impaired fertilization and settlement success in *Acropora palmata* (Albright et al., 2010) and reduced growth and zooxanthellae uptake in juveniles (Suwa et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4277 ---
Most corals studied have shown negative relationships between acidification and growth (Table 3.2.2), and acidification is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007, Silverman et al. 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4278 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 4279 ---
There is little species-specific information, although in general *Acropora* species are moderately to highly susceptible to disease.

--- SENTENCE 4280 ---
Susceptibility and impacts of disease on *Acropora globiceps* are not known.

--- SENTENCE 4281 ---
However, ample evidence show that diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species (e.g., (Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009)), and there is evidence that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Green and Bruckner, 2000; Sutherland et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 4282 ---
The specific effects of predation are poorly known for *Acropora globiceps*.

--- SENTENCE 4283 ---
Most *Acropora* are preferentially consumed by crown-of-thorns seastars (*Acanthaster planci*) (Colgan, 1987) and by corallivorous snails (B. Vargas-Ángel, CRED, Honolulu, HI, pers.

--- SENTENCE 4284 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):**

--- SENTENCE 4285 ---
The specific effects of LBSP stresses are largely unknown for *Acropora globiceps*.

--- SENTENCE 4286 ---
LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually,and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 4287 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 4288 ---
As a whole, the genus *Acropora* has been heavily involved in international trade with 50,000– 270,000 reported exported pieces per year from Indonesia (CITES, 2010).

Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Acropora globiceps* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 4290 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora globiceps* include the relatively high susceptibility of the genus *Acropora* to common threats (bleaching, acidification, disease, predation, and pollution), its restricted depth range (0-8 m), and narrow geographic and latitudinal distribution.

--- SENTENCE 4291 ---
The high bleaching rate of acroporid corals is the primary known threat of extinction for *Acropora globiceps*.

--- SENTENCE 4292 ---
Factors that reduce the potential extinction risk (decrease likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora globiceps* were the reports of common abundance and persistence in intertidal habitats, suggesting potentially increased physiological tolerance.

--- SENTENCE 4293 ---
Wide geographic range was considered to decrease extinction risk, since it makes the species more likely to escape stresses or catastrophes in at least some locations.

--- SENTENCE 4294 ---

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora horrida* are usually open branched, becoming bushy on upper reef slopes and in shallow lagoons.

--- SENTENCE 4300 ---
Main branches of colonies in turbid water have irregular branchlets; those in shallow clear water have compact branchlets, giving colonies a bushy appearance.

--- SENTENCE 4301 ---
Corallites are irregular and the surface of branches is rough.

--- SENTENCE 4302 ---
Tentacles are usually extended during the day.

--- SENTENCE 4303 ---
Colonies are usually pale blue (which may photograph pink or purple), sometimes dark blue or pale yellow or brown.

--- SENTENCE 4304 ---
Polyps are pale blue or white (Veron, 2000).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: *Acropora horrida* is similar to *Acropora tortuosa*, and also to *Acropora vaughani*, which has widely-spaced corallites and a smooth coenosteum (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4305 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: Fossil records of *Acropora horrida* dating back to the Pliocene (1.8–5.3 Ma) were reported from Papua New Guinea (Wallace, 1999).

####

--- SENTENCE 4306 ---
**Global Distribution**

*Acropora horrida* has been reported to have large longitudinal and latitudinal ranges.

--- SENTENCE 4307 ---
Reported ranges include the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, the southwest and northwest Indian Ocean, the Arabian/Iranian Gulf, the northern Indian Ocean, the central Indo-Pacific, east and west coasts of Australia, Southeast Asia, Japan and the East China Sea, the oceanic west Pacific, and the central Pacific (IUCN, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4308 ---
It is found in Palau (Randall, 1995) and the Line Islands (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4309 ---
*Acropora horrida* has a very broad range overall, having the 14th largest range of 114 *Acropora* species examined (Richards, 2009).

**Life History**

*Acropora horrida* is a hermaphroditic spawner (Babcock et al., 1994;

--- SENTENCE 4319 ---
Baird et al., 2002; Kenyon, 1995) with lecithotrophic larvae (Baird et al., 2009), although spawning may be asynchronyous in some areas (Baird et al., 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4320 ---
Mean egg size for *Acropora horrida* has been recorded as 0.64 mm and mean polyp fecundity has been recorded as 9.0 eggs per polyp (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4321 ---
This species did not spawn on the central Great Barrier Reef during the major multispecies spawning events in early summer 1981-1983.

--- SENTENCE 4322 ---
Colonies of this species in which gametogenesis did not proceed to completion differed from those in which it did in two ways: they were in deeper water and they underwent chronic fragmentation and partial burial.

--- SENTENCE 4323 ---
It is possible that their resources were at all times allocated to extension in preference to sexual reproduction (Wallace, 1985).

For more genus level information, see Section 7.5 "Genus *Acropora*."

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora jacquelineae* are flat plates up to 1 m in diameter.

--- SENTENCE 4354 ---
Viewed from above, plates are covered with a mass of fine delicately-curved axial corallites giving an almost moss-like appearance.

--- SENTENCE 4355 ---
There is almost no development of radial corallites.

--- SENTENCE 4356 ---
Colonies are uniform grey-brown or pinkish in color (Veron, 2000).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: Genetic analyses among 35 *Acropora* spp.

--- SENTENCE 4357 ---
examining variation in both mitochondrial (mt control region) and nuclear (PaxC) markers indicates that *Acropora jacquelineae* is polyphyletic for the mitochondrial marker, but monophyletic for the nuclear marker (Richards et al., 2008b).

--- SENTENCE 4358 ---
This pattern, along with evidence of some allele sharing with other species, is consistent with *Acropora jacquelineae* having a complex, reticulate evolutionary history including introgression, but does not provide strong evidence that it consititues a 'hybrid species' as is shown for other *Acropora* spp.

--- SENTENCE 4359 ---
in Richards' analysis (Richards et al., 2008b), none of which are candidate coral species considered in this Status Review Report.

--- SENTENCE 4360 ---
Hence, the BRT considered *Acropora jacquelineae* as a valid species.

--- SENTENCE 4361 ---
*Acropora jacquelineae* is similar to *Acropora paniculata* which has larger corallites (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4362 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: No fossil records of *Acropora jacquelineae* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

#### **Global Distribution**

*Acropora jacquelineae* has been reported from the central Indo-Pacific (IUCN, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4364 ---

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora listeri* are irregular clumps or corymbose plates with thick branches of highly irregular length and shape.

--- SENTENCE 4415 ---
Branches may be tapered (in wave-washed habitats), conical, dome-shaped or globular (in less-exposed habitats), depending upon the degree of formation of axial corallites.

--- SENTENCE 4416 ---
One or more axial corallites may occur on branch ends or, commonly, there are no axial corallites.

--- SENTENCE 4417 ---
Radial corallites are irregularly immersed to tubular and often have slit-like openings and pointed rims, giving colonies a spiny appearance.

--- SENTENCE 4418 ---
Colonies are cream or brown in color (Veron, 2000).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 4419 ---
"Like *Acropora polystoma*, this species is not easily identified in the field and it appears to be restricted to reef edge situations" (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4420 ---
*Acropora listeri* is similar to *Acropora polystoma*, which has welldefined axial corallites; it does not form dome-shaped or globular branches and has less irregular radial corallites.

--- SENTENCE 4421 ---
It is also similar to *Acropora lutkeni* (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4422 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: Fossil records of *Acropora listeri* have been reported from the Pleistocene (1.8– 0.01 Ma) from Niue (Wallace, 1999).

####

--- SENTENCE 4423 ---
**Global Distribution**

*Acropora listeri* has been reported from the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden (questionable according to Veron 2000), the northern Indian Ocean, the central Indo-Pacific, east and west coasts of Australia, Southeast Asia, Japan and the East China Sea, the oceanic west Pacific, and the central Pacific (IUCN, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4424 ---
It has also been found in Mauritius (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4425 ---
*Acropora listeri* has a very broad range overall, having the 13th largest range of 114 Acropora species examined (Richards, 2009).

*Acropora listeri* is a hermaphroditic spawner (Baird et al., 2010;

--- SENTENCE 4435 ---
Harrison et al., 1984) with lecithotrophic larvae (Baird et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4436 ---
For more genus level information, see Section 7.5: Genus *Acropora*.

#### **Threats**

For each of these possible threats, see also Section 7.5: *Genus Acropora* for additional genus level information.

--- SENTENCE 4437 ---
Although there is not much species-specific information about the response of *Acropora listeri* to thermal stress, the genus *Acropora* are consistently ranked among the coral genera most severely susceptible to bleaching (Marshall and Baird, 2000; McClanahan et al., 2007; McClanahan et al., 2005a).

--- SENTENCE 4438 ---
However, the genus may have differential responses across regions during mass bleaching mortalities (McClanahan et al., 2004a).

--- SENTENCE 4439 ---
*Acropora listeri* has moderate to high bleaching susceptibility among *Acropora* (Done et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 4440 ---
No specific research has addressed the effects of acidification on *Acropora listeri*, but experiments on acidification have demonstrated negative effects on *Acropora* calcification (Anthony et al., 2008;

--- SENTENCE 4441 ---
Marubini et al., 2003; Renegar and Riegl, 2005; Schneider and Erez, 2006) and productivity (Anthony et al., 2008; Crawley et al., 2010), as well as impaired fertilization and settlement success in *Acropora palmata* (Albright et al., 2010) and reduced growth and zooxanthellae uptake in juveniles (Suwa et al., 2010)*.*

--- SENTENCE 4442 ---
Most corals studied have shown negative relationships between acidification and growth (Table 3.2.2), and acidification is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007;

--- SENTENCE 4443 ---
Silverman et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4444 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have already caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 4445 ---
In general, *Acropora* species are moderately to highly susceptible to disease.

--- SENTENCE 4446 ---
Specific susceptibility and impacts of disease on this species are not known.

--- SENTENCE 4447 ---
However, ample evidence show that diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species, particularly acroporids (e.g., Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009), and there is evidence that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Sutherland et al., 2004; Green and Bruckner, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4448 ---
The specific effects of predation are poorly known for *Acropora listeri*.

--- SENTENCE 4449 ---
Most *Acropora* are preferentially consumed by crown-of-thorns seastars (*Acanthaster planci*) (Colgan, 1987) and by corallivorous snails (B. Vargas-Ángel, CRED, Honolulu, HI, pers.

--- SENTENCE 4450 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):**

--- SENTENCE 4451 ---
The specific effects of LBSP stresses are largely unknown for *Acropora listeri*.

--- SENTENCE 4452 ---
LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually, and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 4453 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 4454 ---
As a whole, the genus *Acropora* has been heavily involved in international trade with 50,000– 270,000 reported exported pieces per year from Indonesia (CITES, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4456 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora listeri* include the relatively high susceptibility of the genus *Acropora* to common threats (bleaching, acidification, disease, predation, and pollution), a Richards' Occupancy Type 2 (see Section 7.5: Genus *Acropora*) with large global distribution, limited local distribution, uncommon local abundance—these characteristics tend toward species local extinction (Richards, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4457 ---

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora lokani* are composed of robust horizontal main branches that usually diverge.

--- SENTENCE 4466 ---
Short upright branchlets diverge from main branches.

--- SENTENCE 4467 ---
Axial corallites and incipient axial corallites radiate from branchlets and are tubular in shape and large.

--- SENTENCE 4468 ---
Radial corallites are small and pocket shaped.

--- SENTENCE 4469 ---
Colonies are cream, brown or blue (which may photograph pink) in color (Veron, 2000).

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 4470 ---
*Acropora lokani* is similar to *Acropora caroliniana* which has smaller corallites and *Acropora granulosa* (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4471 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: No fossil records of *Acropora lokani* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4473 ---
comm., April 2010 but see below), Pohnpei, Solomons (IUCN, 2010), Raja Ampat, Coral Sea and the Great Barrier Reef (D. Fenner, pers.

--- SENTENCE 4474 ---

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora microclados* are corymbose plates up to approximately 1 m across, with short, uniform, evenlyspaced, tapered branchlets up to 10 mm thick at the base.

--- SENTENCE 4518 ---
Axial corallites are tubular and conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 4519 ---
Incipient axial corallites are common.

--- SENTENCE 4520 ---
Radial corallites are irregular, mostly tubular and appressed, with sharp-edged nariform openings.

--- SENTENCE 4521 ---
Colonies are usually a distinctive pale pinkish-brown in color but are occasionally other colors.

--- SENTENCE 4522 ---
Pale grey tentacles are often extended during the day (Veron, 2000; Veron and Wallace, 1984).

--- SENTENCE 4523 ---
Determinate growth.

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 4524 ---
*Acropora microclados* is most similar to *Acropora massawensis*, which forms prostrate colonies and has less tubular radial corallites, *Acropora lamarcki*, which has less exsert and less tubular radial corallites, and *Acropora macrostoma*, which does not have nariform corallite openings (Veron and Wallace, 1984).

--- SENTENCE 4525 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: No fossil records of *Acropora microclados* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

#### **Global Distribution**

*Acropora microclados* has been reported across a wide distribution ranging from the Red Sea, the central and western Indian Ocean, to the central Indo-Pacific, west and east coasts of Australia, Southeast Asia, Japan and the East China Sea (Veron, 2000; Veron and Wallace, 1984).

J. Maragos (USFWS, Honolulu, HI, pers.

comm., April 2010) has confirmed its presence in the central Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 4577 ---

--- SENTENCE 4592 ---
For more genus level information, see Section 7.5: Genus *Acropora*.

#### **Threats**

For each of these possible threats, see also Section 7.5:

--- SENTENCE 4593 ---
Genus *Acropora* for additional genus level information.

--- SENTENCE 4594 ---
Although there is not much species-specific information about the response of *Acropora palmerae* to thermal stress, the genus *Acropora* are consistently ranked among the coral genera most severely susceptible to bleaching (Marshall and Baird, 2000; McClanahan et al., 2007; McClanahan et al., 2005a).

--- SENTENCE 4595 ---
However, the genus may have differential responses across regions during mass bleaching mortalities (McClanahan et al., 2004a).

--- SENTENCE 4596 ---
No specific research has addressed the effects of acidification on *Acropora palmerae*, but experiments on acidification impacts have demonstrated negative effects on *Acropora* calcification (Anthony et al., 2008;

--- SENTENCE 4597 ---
Marubini et al., 2003; Renegar and Riegl, 2005; Schneider and Erez, 2006) and productivity (Anthony et al., 2008; Crawley et al., 2010), as well as impaired fertilization and settlement success in *Acropora palmata* (Albright et al., 2010) and reduced growth and zooxanthellae uptake in juveniles (Suwa et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4598 ---
Most corals studied have shown negative relationships between acidification and growth (Table 3.2.2), and acidification is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007;

--- SENTENCE 4599 ---
Silverman et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 4600 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have already caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 4601 ---
**Disease:** Susceptibility and impacts of disease on *Acropora palmerae* are not known, although in general *Acropora* species are moderately-to-highly susceptible to disease.

--- SENTENCE 4602 ---
However, ample evidence show that diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species (e.g., Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009), and there is evidence that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Sutherland et al., 2004; Green and Bruckner, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4603 ---
The specific effects of predation are poorly known for *Acropora palmerae*.

--- SENTENCE 4604 ---
Most *Acropora* are preferentially consumed by crown-of-thorns seastars (*Acanthaster planci*) (Colgan, 1987) and by corallivorous snails (B. Vargas-Ángel, CRED, Honolulu, HI, pers.

--- SENTENCE 4605 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):**

--- SENTENCE 4606 ---
The specific effects of LBSP stresses are largely unknown for *Acropora palmerae*.

--- SENTENCE 4607 ---
LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 4608 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 4609 ---
As a whole, the genus *Acropora* has been heavily involved in international trade with 50,000– 270,000 reported exported pieces per year from Indonesia (CITES, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 4611 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora palmerae* include the relatively high susceptibility of the genus *Acropora* to common threats (bleaching, acidification, disease, predation, and pollution) and uncommon abundance.

--- SENTENCE 4612 ---
The high bleaching rate of acroporid corals is the primary known threat of extinction for *Acropora palmerae*.

--- SENTENCE 4613 ---
Factors that reduce the potential extinction risk (decrease likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Acropora palmerae* were the moderate geographic and depth distributions, tolerance for high-energy and intertidal habitats, and the potential for higher than reported abundance based on species uncertainty, i.e., it could be a strong-water form of the more common *Acropora robusta*.

--- SENTENCE 4614 ---
Wide geographic distribution was considered to reduce extinction risk by increasing the likelihood that the species would evade stresses and/or catastrophes in at least some locations.

--- SENTENCE 4615 ---
The overall likelihood that *Acropora palmerae* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be in the "more likely than not" risk category with a mean likelihood of 52% and a standard error (SE) of 9% (Fig. 7.5.50).

--- SENTENCE 4616 ---
This SE was calculated by taking the standard deviation of the seven mean voting scores of the BRT members and shows the coherence among the BRT.

--- SENTENCE 4617 ---
The uncertainty of the BRT is reflected in the wide range of votes of 10%–90% (Fig. 7.5.50) and the average range of likelihood estimates of the seven BRT voters (60%).

--- SENTENCE 4618 ---
The overall range of votes reflects the uncertainty among BRT members about the species taxonomy and the lack of ecological and demographic information for *Acropora palmerae*.

#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Acropora paniculata* are large plates or tables that are 25 mm thick and frequently greater than 1 m across.

--- SENTENCE 4621 ---
Branchlets are short and compact.

--- SENTENCE 4622 ---

--- SENTENCE 4623 ---
Radial corallites are immersed on lower branchlets.

--- SENTENCE 4624 ---
Colonies are cream, grey or blue in color (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4625 ---
Maximum colony size is 200 cm.

--- SENTENCE 4626 ---
Determinate growth.

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 4627 ---

--- SENTENCE 4628 ---
It is quite similar to *Acropora cytherea*, but more delicate in structure (Wallace, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4629 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history:**

--- SENTENCE 4630 ---
No fossil records of *Acropora paniculata* have been reported (Wallace, 1999).

*Acropora paniculata* has been reported across a wide distribution ranging from the Red Sea and Indian Ocean (Chagos), to the west and central Pacific with some range discrepancies between IUCN and Veron (IUCN, 2010; Veron, 2000).

comm., April 2010), Rodrigues (Fenner et al., 2004) and Society Islands (Wallace, 1999).

*Acropora pharaonis* photos and corallite plan from Veron (2000).
