- Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument (Nihoa, Necker, French Frigate Shoals, Gardner Pinnacles, Maro Reef, Laysan, Lisianski, Pearl and Hermes, Midway)
- Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument (Johnston, Kingman)
- Kaloko-Honokōhau National Historic Park, Hawai`i
- Puukoholā Heiau National Historic Site, Hawai`i
- Kalaupapa National Historic Park, Molokai
- Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary

#### **Habitat**

**Habitat:** *Cyphastrea ocellina* has been reported to occupy upper reef slopes (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7281 ---
Stimson (1978) reported *Cyphastrea ocellina* in shallow water only—reef flats, tide pools, and vertical rock in turbid shallow water.

--- SENTENCE 7282 ---
Wright (1986) reported that *Cyphastrea ocellina* typically colonizes dead substrate.

--- SENTENCE 7283 ---
According to an IUCN Red List report, the species is found on shallow upper reef slopes, lagoons, and outer channels (IUCN, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 7284 ---
Jokiel et al. (2007) reported the species on reef flats, reef crest, and fore reefs.

--- SENTENCE 7285 ---
**Depth range**: *Cyphastrea ocellina* has been reported in water depths ranging from 5 m to 20 m (Carpenter et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 7286 ---
#### **Abundance**

Abundance of *Cyphastrea ocellina* has been reported as rare (Veron, 2000) or uncommon (Carpenter et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 7287 ---
It is not common in Hawai`i, but is found commonly enough that most of the physiology of the species is known from that location.

#### **Life History**

*Cyphastrea ocellina* is a simultaneous hermaphrodite (Kolinski and Cox, 2003; Wright, 1986) that broods freeswimming, tentaculate, zooxanthellate planula larvae with distinctive white bodies at the oral end (Edmondson, 1929).

--- SENTENCE 7288 ---
Planulae are produced continuously and released year-round; planulation may be in phase with the new moon (Stimson, 1978) or unrelated to lunar phase (Edmondson, 1946).

--- SENTENCE 7289 ---
Colonies become gravid at a size of ~ 6 cm2 (Stimson, 1978), but are less fecund than other brooders like *Pocillopora damicornis* (Wright, 1986), resulting in lower larval concentrations in the water column (Hodgson, 1985) and consequently, relative scarcity of *Cyphastrea ocellina* (Fitzhardinge, 1993).

--- SENTENCE 7290 ---
*Cyphastrea ocellina* larvae contain zooxanthellae (Wright, 1986).

--- SENTENCE 7291 ---
Planulae can settle after 3 days, or remain unattached for over a month (Edmondson, 1929).

--- SENTENCE 7292 ---
Settled larvae tend to aggregate (Edmondson, 1946).

--- SENTENCE 7293 ---
Settled *Cyphastrea ocellina* can survive for up to 4 months without feeding, although skeletal deposition is reduced under these conditions (Edmondson, 1929).

--- SENTENCE 7294 ---
Planulae can tolerate elevated temperatures; settled larvae can deposit skeletal material at elevated temperatures (30°C–31.5°C), but do not show high survival (Edmondson, 1929).

--- SENTENCE 7295 ---
Planulae can also tolerate brief periods (several days) of reduced salinity more effectively than Pocilloporid larvae (Edmondson, 1929) but die quickly in fresh water (Edmondson, 1946).

--- SENTENCE 7296 ---
*Cyphastrea ocellina* larvae can settle in acidic water (pH = 6) but do not survive (Edmondson, 1946).

--- SENTENCE 7297 ---
Feeding responses (mouth opening, extension of mesenterial filaments) of *Cyphastrea ocellina* are stimulated by both live prey and amino acid extracts and peptides (Mariscal and Lenhoff, 1968).

--- SENTENCE 7298 ---
Lipid levels (~ 40% of dry tissue weight) in shallow-water *Cyphastrea ocellina* are at the higher end of the range found in Hawaiian corals, potentially serving as an energy reserve during stressful conditions (Stimson, 1987).

--- SENTENCE 7299 ---
Growth is generally slow after settlement, often requiring 4 months to produce the first bud, with larger colonies growing ~ 2 mm/yr (Edmondson, 1929).

--- SENTENCE 7300 ---
More recent work shows faster growth rates—4.0 mm in 11 months (Romano, 1990), or as much as 1.4 cm/yr (pers.

--- SENTENCE 7301 ---
Colonies, after 39 months of observation, reached a maximum size of 68.7 mm (Fitzhardinge, 1993).

--- SENTENCE 7302 ---
*Cyphastrea ocellina* shows high aggression.

--- SENTENCE 7303 ---
It generally has a halo growing around it, often even excluding algae (Fitzhardinge, 1993).

--- SENTENCE 7304 ---
*Cyphastrea ocellina* uses extracoelenteric digestion to defend itself against faster-growing corals, but at a high energetic cost that reduces growth rates (Romano, 1990).

#### **Threats**

**Thermal stress:**

--- SENTENCE 7305 ---
The genus *Cyphastrea* is generally resistant to bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 7306 ---
The genus was unaffected during the 1998 mass bleaching in the Great Barrier Reef (Marshall and Baird, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7307 ---
However, elevated temperatures can still induce mortality in *Cyphastrea* even in the absence of bleaching (McClanahan, 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7308 ---
In Hawai`i *Cyphastrea ocellina* contains Clade C1 zooxanthellae (Thornhill, 2003), which may be relatively bleaching-tolerant (Smith et al., 2004b).

--- SENTENCE 7309 ---
Unknown for this genus *Cyphastrea*.

--- SENTENCE 7310 ---
However, in most corals studied (Table 3.2.2), acidification impairs growth (Langdon and Atkinson, 2005; Manzello, 2010) and, in the case of *Acropora palmata*, impairs fertilization and settlement success (Albright et al., 2010) and is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007; Silverman et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7311 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7312 ---
Unknown, but its congeners have been infected with diseases.

--- SENTENCE 7313 ---
*Cyphastrea chalcidicum* is susceptible to ciliateinduced skeletal-eroding band (Antonius and Lipscomb, 2000), while *Cyphastrea microphthalma* in the United Arab Emirates have contracted yellow-band disease (Korrubel and Riegl, 1998).

--- SENTENCE 7314 ---
The ecological and population impacts of disease have not been established for *Cyphastrea ocellina*.

--- SENTENCE 7315 ---
However, ample evidence indicate that diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species (e.g., Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009) and evidence show that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Green and Bruckner, 2000; Sutherland et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7316 ---
Unknown for *Cyphastrea ocellina*.

--- SENTENCE 7317 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):** *Cyphastrea ocellina* may not compete well at high nutrient loads.

--- SENTENCE 7318 ---
The species rapidly recovered after sewage diversion reduced nutrient loads in Kāne`ohe Bay (Maragos et al., 1985) but rapidly crashed again during the *Dictyosphaeria cavernosa* bloom in 1990 (Evans, 1995).

LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 7319 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 7320 ---
This coral experiences light to moderate trade at the genus level (CITES, 2010).

--- SENTENCE 7321 ---
From 1993 to 2008, an average of 248 specimens were exported worldwide, although the majority of the trade is accounted for by an export of 2810 specimens from Indonesia in 1993.

--- SENTENCE 7322 ---
Only a single specimen identified as *Cyphastrea ocellina* was exported in 2002 (CITES, 2010).

!

--- SENTENCE 7323 ---
Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Cyphastrea ocellina* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7324 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Cyphastrea ocellina* are that it has experienced population fluctuations in the past resulting from LBSP stress.

--- SENTENCE 7325 ---
Factors that reduce potential extinction risk (decrease the likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) are that *Cyphastrea ocellina* is likely relatively resistant to bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 7326 ---
Its life history and physiology may help it resist or recover from disturbance.

--- SENTENCE 7327 ---
The overall likelihood that *Cyphastrea ocellina* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be in the "less likely than not" risk category with a mean likelihood of 47% and a standard error (SE) of 14% (Fig. 7.21.8).

--- SENTENCE 7328 ---
This SE was calculated by taking the standard deviation of the seven mean voting scores of the BRT members and shows the coherence among the BRT.

--- SENTENCE 7329 ---
The uncertainty of the BRT is reflected in the range of votes of 10%–90% (Fig. 7.21.8) and the average range of likelihood estimates of the seven BRT voters (52%).

--- SENTENCE 7330 ---
The overall wide range of votes reflects the uncertainty among BRT members inherent in the lack of adequate ecological and demographic information for *Cyphastreaocellina.*

#### **7.22 Genus** *Euphyllia* **(Family Caryophyllidae)**

**7.22.1** *Euphyllia cristata* **Chevalier, 1971** 

!

--- SENTENCE 7331 ---
*Euphyllia cristata* photos and corallite plan from Veron (2000).

--- SENTENCE 7332 ---
#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Euphyllia cristata* are phaceloid, comprised of branching separate corallites.

--- SENTENCE 7333 ---
Corallites are closely compacted, 20 mm–40 mm diameter.

--- SENTENCE 7334 ---
Small solitary polyps are common.

--- SENTENCE 7335 ---
Primary septa are very exsert and are conspicuous underwater.

--- SENTENCE 7336 ---
First and second order septa plunge steeply near the centre of the corallite.

--- SENTENCE 7337 ---
There are no columellae.

--- SENTENCE 7338 ---
Polyps have large tubular tentacles with knob-like tips.

--- SENTENCE 7339 ---
Polyps are usually pale grey or green, with distinctively colored tips to the tentacles (Veron, 2000).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues:**

--- SENTENCE 7340 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: The genus is known from the Oligocene Epoch in the Tethys Sea and Caribbean but is extinct in those locations; known from the Eocene Age in Eurasia and the Indo-Pacific (Wells and Moore, 1956).

#### **Global Distribution**

*Euphyllia cristata* has a moderately wide range, including higher latitude areas in the Ryukus (Japan) and along both coasts of Australia.

--- SENTENCE 7341 ---
IUCN reports its existence off east Africa while Veron (2000) does not.

--- SENTENCE 7342 ---
It ranges east into the central Pacific.

!

--- SENTENCE 7343 ---
*Euphyllia cristata* distribution from IUCN copied from http://www.iucnredlist.org.

!

--- SENTENCE 7344 ---
*Euphyllia cristata* distribution from Veron (2000).

#### **U.S. Distribution**

According to the IUCN Species Account, *Euphyllia cristata* occurs in American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

--- SENTENCE 7345 ---
The CITES database does not list its occurrence in U.S. waters.

--- SENTENCE 7346 ---
A search of published and unpublished records of occurrence in U.S. waters indicates *Euphyllia cristata* has been reported from Tutuila in American Samoa (CRED, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 7347 ---
data) and Guam (Randall, 2003).

--- SENTENCE 7348 ---
Within federally protected waters, *Euphyllia cristata* has been recorded from:

War in the Pacific National Historical Park, Guam.

#### **Habitat**

**Habitat:** Veron (2000) describes *Euphyllia cristata* as inhabiting shallow reef habitats, while the IUCN account includes a wide depth range (see below).

--- SENTENCE 7349 ---
**Depth range**: *Euphyllia cristata* occurs at depths of 1 m to 35 m (IUCN Species Account).

--- SENTENCE 7350 ---
#### **Abundance**

Abundance of *Euphyllia cristata* has been reported to be from common (Carpenter et al., 2008) to uncommon but conspicuous (Veron, 2000).

####

--- SENTENCE 7351 ---
**Life History**

Reproductive mode is not known for *Euphyllia cristata*.

--- SENTENCE 7352 ---
One congener (*Euphyllia ancora*) is a gonochoric spawner (Guest et al., 2005a;

--- SENTENCE 7353 ---
Willis et al., 1985) while another congener (*Euphyllia glabrescens*) is reported to be a hermaphroditic brooder in southern Taiwan (Fan et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7354 ---
No other information regarding its ecology or life history is available.

#### **Threats**

**Thermal stress**: *Euphyllia* species experienced high bleaching but mortality is unknown following the 1997/1998 mass bleaching event in Palau (Bruno et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 7355 ---
Congener *Euphyllia paraancora* in Taiwan contained both Clades C and D zooxanthellae, with Clade D primarily in stressful environments like shallow waters and reef edges (Chen et al., 2005).

--- SENTENCE 7356 ---
The effects of changes in ocean acidification are largely unknown for the genus *Euphyllia*.

--- SENTENCE 7357 ---
When raised in acidified conditions, congener *Euphyllia paradivisa* showed little change in skeletal morphology, while *Galaxea* and *Stylophora* showed substantial skeletal change and *Pocillopora* died (Tibbits, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7358 ---
However, in most corals studied (Table 3.2.2), acidification impairs growth (Langdon and Atkinson, 2005; Manzello, 2010) and, in the case of *Acropora palmata*, impairs fertilization and settlement success (Albright et al., 2010) and is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007; Silverman et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7359 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7360 ---
**Disease:** Susceptibility and impacts of disease on *Euphyllia cristata* are not known.

--- SENTENCE 7361 ---
However, ample evidence indicate that diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species (e.g., Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009) and evidence show that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Green and Bruckner, 2000; Sutherland et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7362 ---
Unknown for *Euphyllia cristata*.

--- SENTENCE 7363 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):**

--- SENTENCE 7364 ---
The effects of LBSP are largely unknown for the genus *Euphyllia*.

--- SENTENCE 7365 ---
Abundance of *Euphyllia* recruits was enhanced in areas where fish were excluded, indicating it may be more tolerant of the shaded conditions created by increased algal biomass in overfished areas (Hughes et al., 2007).

--- SENTENCE 7366 ---
Congener *Euphyllia divisa* was fairly sensitive to exposure to cyanide; concentrations at or below those used in cyanide fishing caused a progressive tissue detachment, microbial infection, and death (Cervino et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 7367 ---
Large patches of *Euphyllia* sp. can form in turbid areas in Indonesia, suggesting a toleration of high sediment loads (Sandin et al., 2008).

LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 7368 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 7369 ---
**Collection/Trade:** *Euphyllia cristata* is heavily involved in the aquarium trade with species-specific exports or quotas from Indonesia, Fiji, Malaysia, and Tonga.

--- SENTENCE 7370 ---
Actual reported annual exports from Indonesia alone averaged over 36,000 pieces from 2000 to 2008 (CITES, 2010).

!

--- SENTENCE 7371 ---
Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Euphyllia cristata* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7372 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Euphyllia cristata* include its heavy involvement in international trade combined with its rare existence but conspicuous colonies, suggesting it is vulnerable to overexploitation.

--- SENTENCE 7373 ---
*Euphyllia cristata* appears to be susceptible to bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 7374 ---
Its geographic distribution range is moderate, although wider than its congeners under consideration in this review.

--- SENTENCE 7375 ---
Wide distribution lowers extinction risk by making it more likely a species will be able to escape the impacts of threats and catastrophes in at least some locations.

--- SENTENCE 7376 ---
The overall likelihood *Euphyllia cristata* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be in the "more likely than not" risk category with a mean likelihood of 62% and a standard error (SE) of 11% (Fig. 7.22.4).

--- SENTENCE 7379 ---
The overall wide range of votes reflects the uncertainty among BRT members inherent in the lack of adequate ecological and demographic information for *Euphyllia cristata*.

#### **Characteristics**

--- SENTENCE 7382 ---
Several species in this genus (including *Euphyllia glabrescens*, *Euphyllia paraglabrescens*, and *Euphyllia paradivisa*) cannot be distinguished based on skeletal characters, but only by the characters of polyp tentacles.

--- SENTENCE 7383 ---

--- SENTENCE 7384 ---

--- SENTENCE 7385 ---
Tentacle tips form concentric circles.

--- SENTENCE 7386 ---
Generally, colonies are pale tan or greenish-brown in color (Veron, 2000).

Abundance of *Euphyllia* recruits was enhanced in areas where fish were excluded, indicating it may be more tolerant of the shaded conditions created by increased algal biomass in overfished areas (Hughes et al., 2007).

--- SENTENCE 7466 ---
Congener *Euphyllia divisa* was fairly sensitive to exposure to cyanide; concentrations at or below those used in cyanide fishing caused a progressive tissue detachment, microbial infection, and death (Cervino et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 7467 ---
Large patches of *Euphyllia* sp. can form in turbid areas in Indonesia, suggesting a toleration of high sediment loads (Sandin et al., 2008).

LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 7468 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 7469 ---
are heavily involved in the aquarium trade.

--- SENTENCE 7470 ---
*Euphyllia paradivisa* is specifically listed in the CITES databases with annual export quotas of up to 2380 "maricultured" pieces from Indonesia, although the meaning of "maricultured" is unclear.

--- SENTENCE 7471 ---
While *Euphyllia cristata* is the species listed in most of the wild-collected exports, the overlapping geographic range and the plethora of similar-looking species within this genus suggest that collection and trade may pose some degree of threat to an uncommon but conspicuous species which is in high international demand.

Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Euphyllia paradivisa* include its heavy involvement in international trade combined with its rare existence but conspicuous colonies, suggesting it is vulnerable to overexploitation.

--- SENTENCE 7474 ---
The species appears bleaching-susceptible.

--- SENTENCE 7475 ---
Its geographic distribution is also somewhat restricted, centered in the threat-prone Coral Triangle Region.

#### **7.23 Genus** *Physogyra*

**7.23.1** *Physogyra lichtensteini* **Saville-Kent, 1871** 

!

--- SENTENCE 7483 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* photos from Veron (2000).

####

--- SENTENCE 7484 ---
**Characteristics**

Colonies of *Physogyra lichtensteini* are massive or thick, platy and meandroid forms with short, widely separated valleys and a light coenosteum.

--- SENTENCE 7485 ---
Colonies have large septa that are solid, smooth-edged, exsert, and widely spaced.

--- SENTENCE 7486 ---
During the day, colonies often have a mass of grape-like or bifurcated vesicles that retract when disturbed.

--- SENTENCE 7487 ---
Tentacles are extended only at night.

--- SENTENCE 7488 ---
Colonies are pale grey in color, sometimes dull green (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7489 ---
There are conflicting reports on the maximum size of this species, ranging from 30 cm (Dinesen, 1983) to 150 cm (Veron and Pichon, 1980).

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 7490 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* is similar to *Plerogyra sinuosa* (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7491 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: A recent Indo-Pacific genus with no known fossil record (Wells and Moore, 1956).

#### **Global Distribution**

*Physogyra lichtensteini* has a relatively broad distribution.

--- SENTENCE 7492 ---
It is found in Australia, Indonesia, Japan, Kenya, Madagascar, the Seychelles, the Red Sea, the Arabian Sea, India, the Philippines, and other areas in the west Pacific.

!

--- SENTENCE 7493 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* distribution from IUCN copied from http://www.iucnredlist.org.

!

--- SENTENCE 7494 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* distribution from Veron (2000).

#### **U.S. Distribution**

According to the IUCN Species Account, *Physogyra lichtensteini* occurs in the Northern Mariana Islands, but no supporting reference is given.

--- SENTENCE 7495 ---
The CITES species database does not include any record of occurrence in U.S. waters.

--- SENTENCE 7496 ---
Veron (2000) also lists the species in the Marianas; however, the Marianas record may be an error resulting from inaccurate geographic attribution of photographic evidence (Kenyon et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 7497 ---
comm., 28 February 2010) indicates a number of photos submitted by him to Veron from Palau and the Cook Islands, and other locations in the Pacific were mistakenly attributed to Guam (similar to the *errata* later acknowledged by Veron (2002) for *Acanthastrea regularis* and *Porites napopora*).

--- SENTENCE 7498 ---
No other published or unpublished data sources indicate the occurrence of *Physogyra lichtensteini* elsewhere in U.S. waters.

#### **Habitat**

**Habitat:**

--- SENTENCE 7499 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* has been reported to occupy turbid reef environments (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7500 ---
The species is common in protected habitats (crevices and overhangs), especially in turbid water with tidal currents (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7501 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* is also reported to be a caverniculous species that prefers shallow but shaded waters, and it is found in caves on the Great Barrier Reef (Dinesen, 1982).

--- SENTENCE 7502 ---
**Depth range**: *Physogyra lichtensteini* has been reported in water depths ranging from 1 m to 20 m (Carpenter et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 7503 ---
#### **Abundance**

Abundance of *Physogyra lichtensteini* has been reported to be common in protected habitats such as crevices and overhangs, especially in turbid water with tidal currents (Veron, 2000).

####

--- SENTENCE 7504 ---
**Life History**

*Physogyra lichtensteini* is a gonochoric broadcast spawner (Babcock et al., 1986;

--- SENTENCE 7505 ---
Willis et al., 1985).

--- SENTENCE 7506 ---
Larvae are lecithotropic, i.e, they do not contain zooxanthellae (Baird et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7507 ---
The minimum size and estimated age of first reproduction have not been determined for any members of the family (Harrison and Wallace, 1990).

--- SENTENCE 7508 ---
Larval longevity has not been determined in this family.

#### **Threats**

**Thermal stress:**

--- SENTENCE 7509 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* has been identified as vulnerable to extinction due to its high bleaching rate, low diversity of its genus, and narrow habitat range (McClanahan et al., 2007).

--- SENTENCE 7510 ---
The species bleached at 31°C in Palau in 1998 (Bruno et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 7511 ---
*Physogyra lichtensteini* contains Clade C zooxanthellae in the South China Sea (Dong et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7512 ---
Unknown for the genus *Physogyra*.

--- SENTENCE 7513 ---
However, in most corals studied (Table 3.2.2), acidification impairs growth (Langdon and Atkinson, 2005; Manzello, 2010) and, in the case of *Acropora palmata*, impairs fertilization and settlement success (Albright et al., 2010) and is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007; Silverman et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7514 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7515 ---
**Disease:** Susceptibility and impacts of disease on *Physogyra lichtensteini* are not known.

--- SENTENCE 7516 ---
However, ample evidence indicates that diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species (e.g., Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009) and evidence show that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Green and Bruckner, 2000; Sutherland et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7517 ---
Population-level effects of predation are unknown for *Physogyra lichtensteini*, although it is preyed upon on by butterflyfish in Indonesia (Nagelkerken et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7518 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):**

--- SENTENCE 7519 ---
The effects of LBSP on *Physogyra lichtensteini* i**s** unknown, but given that it prefers turbid waters the risk of sediment impacts are low.

--- SENTENCE 7520 ---
LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 7521 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 7522 ---
The genus *Physogyra* is heavily traded (CITES, 2010), primarily exported from Indonesia.

--- SENTENCE 7523 ---
Between 1999 and 2010, the trade quota for Indonesia has been on the order of ~ 10,000 specimens annually.

--- SENTENCE 7524 ---
Reported exports for *Physogyra lichtensteini* have been at or near these quotas, averaging 9912 specimens from 1999 to 2008 (CITES, 2010).

Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Physogyra lichtensteini* are that it has a high bleaching rate and is heavily collected.

--- SENTENCE 7527 ---

#### **7.24 Genus** *Turbinaria* **(Family Dendrophylliidae)**

**7.24.1** *Turbinaria mesenterina* **(Lamarck, 1816)

--- SENTENCE 7535 ---
Colonies of *Turbinaria mesenterina* copied from Veron (2000).

--- SENTENCE 7536 ---
#### **Characteristics**

Colonies of *Turbinaria mesenterina* are best known as large lettuce-like assemblages of plates with the polyps or corallites on the upper surfaces (Veron, 2000; see the *Turbinaria mesenterina* illustration in the center).

--- SENTENCE 7537 ---
The plates can be very contorted in shallow depths with a lot of water motion (see the *Turbinaria mesenterina* illustration to the left).

--- SENTENCE 7538 ---
In deeper water or low light conditions, the colonies can be large flat plates (see the *Turbinaria mesenterina* illustration to the right)*.

--- SENTENCE 7539 ---
Turbinaria mesenterina* are usually grey-green or grey-brown in color.

--- SENTENCE 7540 ---
#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 7541 ---
The genus *Turbinaria* is quite distinct and is not confused with other genera.

--- SENTENCE 7542 ---
The species are usually quite distinguishable, especially when seen together.

--- SENTENCE 7543 ---
Some preliminary electrophoretic data suggested species groupings in *Turbinaria* that differ from classic taxonomic definitions (Ayre et al., pers.

--- SENTENCE 7544 ---
in Willis, 1990), although since no further work has been done on the subject they are considered here as valid species.

--- SENTENCE 7545 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: *Turbinaria* originated in the Oligocene Epoch in the Tethys Sea in southern Europe

--- SENTENCE 7546 ---
(Wells and Moore, 1956).

--- SENTENCE 7547 ---
It went extinct in the Atlantic (Caribbean), but it still occurs across the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

#### **Global Distribution**

*Turbinaria mesenterina* has become very broadly distributed both longitudinally from east Africa and the Red Sea to eastern central Pacific and latitudinally from southern Africa and the Great Barrier Reef to Japan.

--- SENTENCE 7548 ---
*Turbinaria mesenterina* has the broadest distribution of the four species of *Turbinaria* considered in this review.

!

--- SENTENCE 7549 ---
*Turbinaria mesenterina* distribution from IUCN copied from http://www.iucnredlist.org.

!

--- SENTENCE 7550 ---
*Turbinaria mesenterina* distribution copied from Veron (2000).

#### **U.S. Distribution**

*Turbinaria mesenterina* is found in Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 7551 ---
The IUCN Red Book lists *Turbinaria mesenteria* in the Marianas Islands, but Randall (1995) does not.

--- SENTENCE 7552 ---
According to both the IUCN Species Account and the CITES species database, *Turbinaria mesenterina* has been recorded in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 7553 ---
The IUCN Species Account also lists its occurrence in the Northern Mariana Islands and U.S. minor outlying islands.

--- SENTENCE 7554 ---
A search of published and unpublished records of occurrence in U.S. waters indicates *Turbinaria mesenterina* has been reported from Tutuila, Ofu-Olosega, and Tau in American Samoa (Lovell and McLardy, 2008; National Park Service, 2009; C. Birkeland, unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 7555 ---
Veron (2000) shows a distribution map including the Northern Mariana Islands (volume 2, page 394) but no independent published or unpublished reference has substantiated this record.

--- SENTENCE 7556 ---
Randall (1995) does not list *Turbinaria mesenterina* for the northern or southern islands in the Mariana Archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 7557 ---
No published or unpublished reference listing its occurrence in the U.S. minor outlying islands could be identified.

--- SENTENCE 7558 ---
Within federally protected waters, *Turbinaria mesenterina* has been recorded from the following areas:

National Park of American Samoa, Ofu Island unit.

--- SENTENCE 7559 ---
#### **Habitat**

**Habitat:** *Turbinaria mesenterina* can be a dominant species, forming massive and extensive stands, especially in shallow protected waters with some turbidity (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7560 ---
*Turbinaria mesenterina* can live on forereef slopes and can prevail in clear water as well, but usually not in areas of heavy wave action.

--- SENTENCE 7561 ---
**Depth range**: The depth range of *Turbinaria mesenterina* has been recorded as 3 m to 20 m (Titlyanov and Latypov, 1991; Veron and Pichon, 1980).

--- SENTENCE 7562 ---
Sheppard and Sheppard (1991) found *Turbinaria mesenterina* to occur commonly "at the base of reef slopes at 10 m or deeper.

--- SENTENCE 7563 ---
"

#### **Abundance**

*Turbinaria mesenterina* has been reported to be common (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7564 ---
The species can be locally dominant and form massive and extensive stands, especially in protected shallow turbid waters.

#### **Life History**

The dominant sexual pattern in *Turbinaria mesenterina* is a gonochoric broadcast spawner, with a 1:1 sex ratio.

--- SENTENCE 7565 ---
However, a low incidence of hermaphroditism has been documented on the Great Barrier Reef (Babcock et al., 2003; Willis, 1987).

--- SENTENCE 7566 ---
Polyps nearest the growing plate edge are sterile or have lowered fecundity in their first year of growth, higher but sub-mature levels of fecundity after 2 or 3 years' growth, and are only fully fecund in their second spawning season, i.e., regions corresponding to 3 years or older.

--- SENTENCE 7567 ---
The minimum size at first reproduction is 12 cm to 16 cm, with an estimated age of 4 years (Willis, 1987).

--- SENTENCE 7568 ---
Planula larvae do not contain zooxanthellae that can supplement maternal provisioning with energy sources provided by their photosynthesis (Baird et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7569 ---
Larval longevity has not been determined in this genus.

--- SENTENCE 7570 ---
Mean diameter of the corallum at settlement, in laboratory studies, is 900 µm (range 800*–*  1000 µm) (Babcock et al., 2003; Willis et al., 1985).

#### **Threats**

**Thermal stress**: Bleaching in *Turbinaria* varies among regions.

--- SENTENCE 7571 ---
The study by Marshall and Baird (2000) showed *Turbinaria* to be the most resistant to bleaching when responding to high seawater temperatures than any of the other 39 generic groups of scleratinians tested.

--- SENTENCE 7572 ---
*Turbinaria* were moderately vulnerable to bleaching in the western Indian Ocean from 1998 to 2005 (McClanahan et al., 2007), but that varied within that region—the genus bleached more in Mauritius than Kenya in 2004 (McClanahan et al., 2005a) and was one of the genera most resistant to bleaching in South Africa (Floros et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7573 ---
Congeneric species had occasionally high bleaching and mortality occurrences in Palau from 1997 to 1998 (Bruno et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 7574 ---
It may be that some of the mixed bleaching response is determined by whether the stress is temperature- or light-induced, as repeated exposure to high irradiance significantly decreases the energy budget in *Turbinaria*

--- SENTENCE 7575 ---
(Hoogenboom et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7576 ---
Alternatively, spatial differences in bleaching could be due to symbiont presence, as *Turbinaria* can host either Clade C or Clade D zooxanthellae (LaJeunesse et al., 2003; Ulstrup et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7577 ---
A closely-related species, *Turbinaria reniformis,* appears to show a lower percent change in calcification when pCO2 is doubled and tripled compared to the other genera of scleractinians experimentally tested (Kleypas et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7578 ---
*Turbinaria reniformis* showed a 13% reduction in growth in high-CO2 waters, but had no significant changes in skeletal microstructures (Marubini et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 7579 ---
Most corals studied have shown negative relationships between acidification and growth (Table 3.2.2) and acidification is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007;

--- SENTENCE 7580 ---
Silverman et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7581 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7582 ---
A white-syndrome disease has affected *Turbinaria* in Australia since 2000; elevated temperatures appear to significantly increase tissue loss (Dalton et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 7583 ---
Black lesions were also observed on *Turbinaria mesenterina* almost simultaneously with a bleaching event on the Great Barrier Reef (Jones et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7584 ---
Also, ample evidence indicate that diseases can have devastating regional effects on individual coral species (e.g., Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009) and evidence show that these effects are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Green and Bruckner, 2000; Sutherland et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7585 ---
**Predation:** Adult colonies of *Turbinaria* spp.

--- SENTENCE 7586 ---
are almost never eaten by crown-of-thorns seastars (Birkeland and Lucas 1990).

--- SENTENCE 7587 ---
*Turbinaria* are not thought to be eaten by *Phestilla sibogae* (Ritson-Williams et al., 2003), but recent evidence suggests that *Phestilla* can both feed on *Turbinaria* as well as infect it with disease (Dalton and Godwin, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7588 ---
**Land-base sources of pollution (LBSP):** *Turbinaria* spp.

--- SENTENCE 7589 ---
can be dominant in turbid waters.

--- SENTENCE 7590 ---
For both *Turbinaria reniformis* and *Turbinaria peltata*, Sheppard and Sheppard (1991) stated that "It coexists with *Turbinaria mesenterina* and is often found in sedimented conditions."

--- SENTENCE 7591 ---
*Turbinaria mesenterina* maintains photosynthetic and growth rates even under highly turbid conditions (Sofonia and Anthony, 2008) and accumulates significant energy reserves (Anthony, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7592 ---
As a genus, *Turbinaria* are efficient sediment-rejecters (Stafford-Smith and Ormond, 1992), but have been observed to incur partial mortality from sediment during dredging events (Blakeway, 2005).

--- SENTENCE 7593 ---
*Turbinaria* adopt funnelshaped morphologies in turbid environments which localizes sediment effects to small portions of the colony (Riegl et al., 1996).*Turbinaria mesenterina* appears to tolerate low-salinity events, as it survived with little damage the 1991 cyclone floodwaters in the Keppel Islands (Van Woesik et al., 1995).

LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 7594 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 7595 ---
According to CITES records, *Turbinaria* spp. are one of the top 10 genera imported into the United States of America (U.S.A.).

--- SENTENCE 7596 ---
Between 1997 and 2001, more than 63,400 specimens were imported (Wabnitz, 2003) and between 2000 and 2008 around 370,000 pieces (between 30,000 and 50,000 per year) were reportedly exported from Indonesia that appears to be the main exporting country of *Turbinaria* spp.

--- SENTENCE 7597 ---
Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Turbinaria mesenterina* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7598 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Turbinaria mesenterina* include susceptibility to disease and harvesting.

--- SENTENCE 7599 ---
*Turbinaria mesenterina* seems susceptible to disease at high latitudes in Australia.

--- SENTENCE 7600 ---
The aquarium trade appears to be the most immediate threat to populations of *Turbinaria.*

--- SENTENCE 7601 ---
Factors that reduce potential extinction risk (decrease the likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) are that *Turbinaria mesenterina* can be dominant in turbid waters, is remarkably tolerant to seawater warming, low salinity events, lower pH, and predation, and is broadly distributed both latitudinally and longitudinally in the Indo-Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 7602 ---
Wide distribution is considered to lower extinction risk by making it more likely a species will be able to escape the impacts of threats and catastrophes in at least some locations

The overall likelihood that *Turbinaria mesenterina* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be in the "less likely than not" risk category with a mean likelihood of 37% and a standard error (SE) of 10% (Fig. 7.24.4).

--- SENTENCE 7603 ---
This SE was calculated by taking the standard deviation of the seven mean voting scores of the BRT members and shows the coherence among the BRT.

--- SENTENCE 7604 ---
The uncertainty of the BRT is reflected in the range of votes of 1%–66% (Fig. 7.24.4) and the average range of likelihood estimates of the seven BRT voters (45%).

--- SENTENCE 7605 ---
The overall wide range of votes reflects the uncertainty among BRT members inherent in the lack of adequate ecological and demographic information for *Turbinaria mesenterina*.

They can live on forereef slopes and can prevail in clear water as well, but usually not in areas of heavy wave action.

--- SENTENCE 7625 ---
**Depth range**: The depth range of *Turbinaria peltata* has been recorded as 0 m–40 m. Sheppard and Sheppard (1991) found *Turbinaria peltata* to occur commonly "at the base of reef slopes at 10 m or deeper."

#### **Abundance**

*Turbinaria peltata* has been reported to be a common species that can be locally dominant and form massive and extensive stands, especially in protected shallow turbid waters (Veron, 2000).

####

--- SENTENCE 7626 ---
**Life History**

*Turbinaria peltata* is a broadcast spawner (Babcock et al., 1994; Kenyon, 1995), but its sexual pattern (hermaphrodite vs. gonochoric) has not been determined.

--- SENTENCE 7627 ---
However, three other species of *Turbinaria* all are gonochoric, although a low frequency of hermaphroditism has been shown on the Great Barrier Reef in the congener *Turbinaria mesenterina*

--- SENTENCE 7628 ---
The minimum size and estimated age at first reproduction have not been determined for this species.

--- SENTENCE 7629 ---
However, for the congener *Turbinaria mesenterina*, the minimum size at first reproduction is 12 cm to 16 cm, with an estimated age of 4 years (Willis, 1987).

--- SENTENCE 7630 ---
Although specific observations have not been published for this species, the larvae of 2 other *Turbinaria* species studied do not contain zooxanthellae that can supplement maternal provisioning with energy sources provided by their photosynthesis (Baird et al., 2009).

#### **Threats**

**Thermal stress**: Bleaching in *Turbinaria* varies among regions.

--- SENTENCE 7631 ---
The study by Marshall and Baird (2000) showed *Turbinaria* to be the most resistant to bleaching when responding to high seawater temperatures than any of the other 39 generic groups of scleratinians tested.

--- SENTENCE 7632 ---
*Turbinaria* were moderately vulnerable to bleaching in the western Indian Ocean from 1998 to 2005 (McClanahan et al., 2007), but that varied within that region—the genus bleached more in Mauritius than Kenya in 2004 (McClanahan et al., 2005a) and was one of the genera most resistant to bleaching in South Africa (Floros et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7633 ---
Congeneric species had occasionally high bleaching and mortality in Palau in 1997–1998 (Bruno et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 7634 ---
It may be that some of the mixed bleaching response is whether the stress is temperature- or light-induced, as repeated exposure to high irradiance significantly decreases the energy budget in *Turbinaria*

--- SENTENCE 7635 ---
(Hoogenboom et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7636 ---
Alternatively, spatial differences in bleaching could be attributed to symbiont presence, as *Turbinaria* can host either Clade C or Clade D zooxanthellae (LaJeunesse et al., 2003; Ulstrup et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7637 ---
A congener *Turbinaria reniformis* appears to show a lower percent change in calcification when pCO2 is doubled and tripled compared to the other genera of scleractinians experimentally tested (Kleypas et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7638 ---
*Turbinaria reniformis* showed 13% reduction in growth in low-carbonate waters but had no significant changes in skeletal microstructures (Marubini et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 7639 ---
We might predict that this is a generic characteristic.

--- SENTENCE 7640 ---
However, most corals studied have shown negative relationships between acidification and growth (Table 3.2.2) and acidification is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007, Silverman et al. 2009).

--- SENTENCE 7641 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to have caused appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7642 ---
A white-syndrome disease has affected *Turbinaria* in Australia since 2000; elevated temperatures appear to significantly increase tissue loss (Dalton et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 7643 ---
Black lesions were also observed on the closely related *Turbinaria mesenterina* almost simultaneously with a bleaching event on the Great Barrier Reef (Jones et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7644 ---
Ample evidence indicate that diseases can have devastating regional effects on individual coral species (e.g., Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009) and there is evidence that these effects are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Green and Bruckner, 2000; Sutherland et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 7645 ---
**Predation:** Adult colonies of *Turbinaria* spp.

--- SENTENCE 7646 ---
are almost never eaten by crown-of-thorns seastars (Birkeland and Lucas 1990).

--- SENTENCE 7647 ---
*Turbinaria* are not thought to be eaten by *Phestilla sibogae* (Ritson-Williams et al., 2003), but recent evidence suggests that *Phestilla* can both feed on *Turbinaria* as well as infect it with disease (Dalton and Godwin, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7648 ---
**Land-base sources of pollution (LBSP):** *Turbinaria* spp.

--- SENTENCE 7649 ---
can be dominant in turbid waters.

--- SENTENCE 7650 ---
For both *Turbinaria reniformis* and *Turbinaria peltata*, Sheppard and Sheppard (1991) stated that "It coexists with *Turbinaria mesenterina* and is often found in sedimented conditions."

--- SENTENCE 7651 ---
The closely related *Turbinaria mesenteria* maintains photosynthetic and growth rates even under highly turbid conditions (Sofonia and Anthony, 2008) and accumulates significant energy reserves (Anthony, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7652 ---
As a genus, *Turbinaria* are efficient sediment rejecters (Stafford-Smith and Ormond, 1992), but have been observed to incur partial mortality from sediment during dredging events (Blakeway, 2005).

--- SENTENCE 7653 ---
*Turbinaria* adopt funnel-shaped morphologies in turbid environments and tends to localize sediment effects to small portions of the colony (Riegl et al., 1996).

--- SENTENCE 7654 ---
*Turbinaria peltata* appears to tolerate low-salinity events, as it survived with little damage the 1991 cyclone floodwaters in the Keppel Islands (Van Woesik et al., 1995).

--- SENTENCE 7655 ---
LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 7656 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 7657 ---
According to CITES records, *Turbinaria* spp. are one of the top 10 genera imported into the USA.

--- SENTENCE 7658 ---
Between 1997 and 2001, more than 63,400 specimens were imported (Wabnitz, 2003) and between 2000 and 2008 around 370,000 pieces (between 30,000 and 50,000 per year) were reportedly exported from Indonesia that appears to be the main exporting country of *Turbinaria* spp (CITES, 2010).

!

--- SENTENCE 7659 ---
Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Turbinaria peltata* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7660 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Turbinaria peltata* include susceptibility to disease and harvesting.

--- SENTENCE 7661 ---
*Turbinaria peltata* seems susceptible to disease at high latitudes in Australia.

--- SENTENCE 7662 ---
The aquarium trade appears to be the most immediate threat to populations of *Turbinaria.*

--- SENTENCE 7663 ---
Factors that reduce potential extinction risk (decrease the likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) are that *Turbinaria peltata* can be dominant in turbid waters, is remarkably tolerant to seawater warming, low salinity events, lower pH, and predation, and is broadly distributed both latitudinally and longitudinally in the Indo-Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 7664 ---
Wide distribution is considered to lower extinction risk by making it more likely a species will be able to escape the impacts of threats and catastrophes in at least some locations

The overall likelihood that *Turbinaria peltata* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be "less likely than not" with a mean likelihood of 37% probability and a standard error (SE) of 10% (Fig. 7.24.8).

--- SENTENCE 7665 ---
This SE was calculated by taking the standard deviation of the seven mean voting scores of the BRT members and shows the coherence among the BRT.

--- SENTENCE 7666 ---
The uncertainty of the BRT is reflected in the range of votes of 1%–66% (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 7667 ---
and the average range of likelihood estimates of the seven BRT voters (45%).

--- SENTENCE 7668 ---
The overall wide range of votes reflects the uncertainty among BRT members inherent in the lack of adequate ecological and demographic information for *Turbinaria peltata*.

#### **7.24.3** *Turbinaria reniformis* **Bernard, 1896**

!

--- SENTENCE 7669 ---
Colonies of *Turbinaria reniformis* copied from Veron (2000).

#### **Characteristics**

*Turbinaria reniformis* are best known as large lettuce-like assemblages of plates with the polyps or corallites on the upper surfaces of the laminae or leaves or blades or plates (see the *Turbinaria reniformis* illustration to the left).

--- SENTENCE 7670 ---
The plates can be very contorted in shallow depths with a lot of water motion.

--- SENTENCE 7671 ---
In deeper water or low light conditions, the colonies can form large flat plates (see the *Turbinaria reniformis* illustration to the right) (Veron, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 7672 ---
*Turbinaria* are usually grey-green or grey-brown in color, although *Turbinaria reniformis* usually displays some bright yellow, especially at the margins.

#### **Taxonomy**

**Taxonomic issues**: None.

--- SENTENCE 7673 ---
The genus *Turbinaria* is quite distinct and is not confused with other genera.

--- SENTENCE 7674 ---
The species are usually quite distinguishable, especially when seen together.

--- SENTENCE 7675 ---
Some preliminary electrophoretic data suggested species groupings in *Turbinaria* that differ from classic taxonomic definitions (Ayre et al., pers.

--- SENTENCE 7676 ---
in Willis, 1990), but no further work has been done on the subject and so they are considered here as valid species.

--- SENTENCE 7677 ---
**Evolutionary and geologic history**: *Turbinaria* originated in the Oligocene Epoch in the Tethys Sea in southern Europe

--- SENTENCE 7678 ---
(Wells and Moore, 1956).

--- SENTENCE 7679 ---
It went extinct in the Atlantic (Caribbean), but it still occurs across the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

#### **Global Distribution**

*Turbinaria reniformis* has become very broadly distributed both longitudinally (from east Africa and the Red Sea to eastern central Pacific) and latitudinally (from southern Africa and the Great Barrier Reef to Japan).

--- SENTENCE 7680 ---
*Turbinaria reniformis* is absent from eastern Australia and southern Africa.

!

*Turbinaria reniformis* distribution from IUCN copied from http://www.iucnredlist.org.

--- SENTENCE 7682 ---
*Turbinaria reniformis* distribution from Veron (2000).

*Turbinaria reniformis* is found in Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 7684 ---

*Turbinaria* are not thought to be eaten by *Phestilla sibogae* (Ritson-Williams et al., 2003), but recent evidence suggests that *Phestilla* can both feed on *Turbinaria* as well as infect it with disease (Dalton and Godwin, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7774 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP):** Unlike *Turbinaria mesenteria, Turbinaria reniformis,* and *Turbinaria peltata, Turbinaria stellulata* tends to be found in clear water.

--- SENTENCE 7775 ---
can, however, be found in shaded conditions (Dinesen, 1983)—implying some ability to cope with reduced light levels, if not turbidity.

--- SENTENCE 7776 ---
*Turbinaria mesenteria* maintains photosynthetic and growth rates even under highly turbid conditions (Sofonia and Anthony, 2008) and accumulates significant energy reserves (Anthony, 2006).

--- SENTENCE 7777 ---
As a genus, *Turbinaria* are efficient sediment rejecters (Stafford-Smith and Ormond, 1992) but have been observed to incur partial mortality from sediment during dredging events (Blakeway, 2005).

--- SENTENCE 7778 ---
*Turbinaria* adopt funnel-shaped morphologies in turbid environments as a means of localizing sediment impacts to small portions of the colony (Riegl et al., 1996).

--- SENTENCE 7779 ---
However, this is unlikely to be a benefit for *Turbinaria stellulata*, which primarily adopts flattened morphologies.

--- SENTENCE 7780 ---
*Turbinaria stellulata* appears to tolerate low-salinity events, as it survived with little damage the 1991 flood in the Keppel Islands (Van Woesik et al., 1995).

--- SENTENCE 7781 ---
LBSP-related stresses (nutrients, sediment, toxins, and salinity) often act in concert rather than individually and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 7782 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales (particularly important for species with limited range) and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009a; Wooldridge, 2009b).

--- SENTENCE 7783 ---
According to CITES records, *Turbinaria* spp. are one of the top 10 genera imported into the USA.

--- SENTENCE 7784 ---
Between 1997 and 2001, over 63,400 specimens were imported and between 2000 and 2008 around 370,000 pieces (between 30,000 and 50,000 per year) were reportedly exported from Indonesia which appears to be the main exporting country of *Turbinaria* spp.

--- SENTENCE 7785 ---
However, *Turbinaria stellulata* might not be as attractive for the aquarium or curio trade because it does not generally grow in plates or blades.

#### **Risk Assessment**

!

--- SENTENCE 7786 ---
Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Turbinaria stellulata* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7787 ---
A factor that increases the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Turbinaria stellulata* includes disease.

--- SENTENCE 7788 ---
Corals of the genus *Turbinaria* seem susceptible to disease at high latitudes in Australia.

--- SENTENCE 7789 ---
Factors that reduce potential extinction risk (decrease the likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Turbinaria stellulata* are tolerance to seawater warming, low salinity events, lower pH, and predation, and a broad geographic distribution both latitudinally and longitudinally in the Indo-Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 7790 ---
Wide distribution is considered to lower extinction risk by making it more likely a species will be able to escape the impacts of threats and catastrophes in at least some locations.

--- SENTENCE 7791 ---
*Turbinaria stellulata* has a higher risk than its congeners due to its relative intolerance of turbid waters.

--- SENTENCE 7792 ---
The overall likelihood that *Turbinaria stellulata* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be in the "less likely than not" risk category with a mean likelihood of 46% and a standard error (SE) of 6% (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 7793 ---
This SE was calculated by taking the standard deviation of the seven mean voting scores of the BRT members and shows the coherence among the BRT.

--- SENTENCE 7794 ---
The uncertainty of the BRT is reflected in the range of votes of 1%–66% (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 7795 ---
7.24.16) and the average range of likelihood estimates of the seven BRT voters (41%).

--- SENTENCE 7796 ---
The overall wide range of votes reflects the uncertainty among BRT members inherent in the lack of adequate ecological and demographic information for *Turbinaria stellulata*.

#### **8.

--- SENTENCE 7797 ---
SYNTHESIS OF RISK ASSESSMENTS:

--- SENTENCE 7798 ---
TAXONOMIC, REGIONAL, AND THREAT-BASED PATTERNS**

Estimated likelihoods that the status for each of the 82 candidate coral species will fall below their Critical Risk Thresholds by the year 2100 are summarized in Figure 8.1 and Table 8.1.

--- SENTENCE 7799 ---
The candidate coral species are listed by ranked mean likelihood score while the range and relative distribution of points across risk likelihood categories reflect the varying uncertainties in demographic data and the individual Biological Review Team (BRT) members' perception of individual risks to each of the candidate species (Fig. 8.1 and Table 8.1).

--- SENTENCE 7800 ---
The relatively large spread of votes across risk categories for each candidate species primarily reflects the lack of adequate ecological and demographic information for most species.

--- SENTENCE 7801 ---
This resulted in uncertainties within votes by each of the BRT members in perception of that species' risk, as well as differences between BRT members' votes.

--- SENTENCE 7802 ---
On average, each BRT member spread their votes across three (mean 2.98, SD 0.66) risk likelihood categories per species or 53.75% (SD 12.73) likelihood points per species.

--- SENTENCE 7803 ---
The methods used to assess extinction risk, and the uncertainties that are reflected, do not allow for fine-scaled partitioning amongst mean likelihood scores for all of the 82 candidate coral species.

--- SENTENCE 7804 ---
However, characteristics of higher- and lower-ranked species can be discerned, and reflect somewhat greater confidence in the extinction risk status of the respective species.

--- SENTENCE 7805 ---
At one end species were clearly identified to have a relatively higher risk of extinction and at the other end a relatively lower risk of extinction, with a gradation of risk between these.

--- SENTENCE 7806 ---
Species with high estimated likelihoods of their status falling below their Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 had at least some specific information available regarding small population size or declining population trends, combined with some specific or generic information indicating relatively high susceptibility to certain threats (e.g., bleaching or disease).

--- SENTENCE 7807 ---
Several of the highest-ranked (most at risk) species also had indications of very low to negligible recruitment potential.

--- SENTENCE 7808 ---
In contrast, species with lower estimated likelihoods of falling below their Critical Risk Thresholds by 2100 generally had wide geographic ranges, high abundances in at least some locations, and tended to display broad tolerances to environmental conditions, as evidenced by low known susceptibility to threats and/or known occurrence in diverse or marginal habitats.

--- SENTENCE 7809 ---
Many, if not most, species in the middle portion of the risk ranking have wide variances in likelihood points, or a relatively equal distribution of points across multiple categories.

--- SENTENCE 7810 ---
The resulting spread reflects some combination of uncertainties relative to taxonomic status, range, threat susceptibility, and population status and trends.

--- SENTENCE 7811 ---
For species in the middle and lower risk likelihood ranges, the evaluation was based primarily on projecting how high impact threats (i.e., ocean warming, disease, and ocean acidification) would affect the species, as there was little, if any, demographic information.

--- SENTENCE 7812 ---
One other clear pattern in these assessments is that Caribbean species tend to have appreciably higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 7813 ---
This reflects partly the relatively small geographic range size represented by the Caribbean basin (relative to the Indo-Pacific region).

--- SENTENCE 7814 ---
It is also clear that the Caribbean region has already been subject to dramatic, basin-wide declines in coral status, as reflected by the impacts of coral disease and general lack of coral recovery following disturbances.

--- SENTENCE 7815 ---
A similar high risk was given to the one species that likely is restricted to the eastern Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 7816 ---
Ocean warming and coral disease were the threats that were deemed most important in driving Critical Risk Threshold likelihoods for the most at-risk species.

--- SENTENCE 7817 ---
However, the anticipated future impacts of ocean acidification were also deemed by the BRT to represent a substantial risk across almost all of the candidate species.

--- SENTENCE 7818 ---
While the BRT acknowledges the impacts of ocean acidification will vary among taxa, in the current state of knowledge, the BRT was unable to accurately separate taxa with greater or lesser risk from ocean acidification.

Photos of *Millepora boschmai* skeletons used in the description of the species (de Weerdt and Glynn, 1991).

--- SENTENCE 10830 ---
*Millepora boschmai* is a species of hydrocoral in the eastern Pacific that may have already gone extinct as a result of thermal-stress induced bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 10831 ---
While not a candidate species, the BRT determined that it would be valuable to assess the degree of extinction risk in this species to provide context for interpreting the voting results of the candidate species.

--- SENTENCE 10832 ---
#### **Characteristics**

Shape and size: irregularly encrusting base from which arise plate-like outgrowths to 12 cm high and 0.5–1 cm thick.

--- SENTENCE 10833 ---
The plates are somewhat irregular in outline and usually increase in width distally, where they are irregularly, sometimes rather deeply, indented.

--- SENTENCE 10834 ---
Lateral plate-like extensions occasionally develop in between the plates, forming weakly developed box-like frameworks.

--- SENTENCE 10835 ---
Coralla of intermediate size, probably not exceeding 30 cm in overall height, 30 cm in length and 17 cm in width.

--- SENTENCE 10836 ---
Surface is generally smooth, sometimes a little warty (de Weerdt and Glynn, 1991).

####

--- SENTENCE 10837 ---
* Six specimens collected in Sumba and South Sulawesi, Indonesia were recently attributed to this species (Razak and Hoeksema, 2003).

--- SENTENCE 10838 ---
Such an anomalous distribution requires taxonomic follow up to confirm or refute conspecific status.

--- SENTENCE 10839 ---
**Class:** Hydrozoa, Order Milleporina, Family Milleporidae

**Evolutionary and geologic history:**

--- SENTENCE 10840 ---
De Weerdt and Glynn (1991) first described this species from the eastern Pacific where it is one of only a few milleporid species, almost all of which are most closely related to Indo-Pacific forms.

--- SENTENCE 10841 ---
They identified this strong affinity with the Indo-pacific as being either due massive Eocene and Pleistocene extinctions in the eastern Pacific followed by reintroduction of Indo-West Pacific species by long-distance dispersal, or survival of some coral populations in eastern Pacific refugia after the closure of the Isthmus of Panama, providing the source for recolonization of places close enough to these refugia (see Rosen (1988) for a review of the different theories).

#### **Global Distribution**

This species was only found in the Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama (de Weerdt and Glynn, 1991), and most recently specimens from Indonesia were identified as *Millepora boschmai* (Razak and Hoeksema 2003).

--- SENTENCE 10842 ---
Its range is very restricted and highly fragmented.

--- SENTENCE 10843 ---
Before 1983, the species was also reported to occur at Contreras Islands, Secas Islands, Coiba Island and Bahía Honda, Panama (de Weerdt and Glynn, 1991).

--- SENTENCE 10844 ---
No confirmed living animals are known, although animals possibly conspecific with this species have recently been reported from Indonesia.

--- SENTENCE 10845 ---
The species was initially recorded from a single location at Coiba Island, Panama and known only from the Gulf of Chiriqui; that subpopulation was regarded as extinct following the 1982/83 El Niño; however, a second subpopulation was later found off Uva Island.

--- SENTENCE 10846 ---
With the subsequent extinction of the Uva Island subpopulation following the 1997/98 El Niño, this species may now be extinct.

--- SENTENCE 10847 ---
Despite intensive searches no further living specimens have been found within the region.

--- SENTENCE 10848 ---
Observed population decline since 1982 in the eastern Pacific region is therefore estimated as 100% (IUCN 2008).

--- SENTENCE 10849 ---
According to Razak and Hoeksema (2003), *Millepora boschmai* may so far have been overlooked in Indonesia and the Indo-West Pacific because it is relatively rare or because it is not well known (Razak and Hoeksema, 2003).

--- SENTENCE 10850 ---
However, many milleporids are easily confused and separated by relatively small morphological characteristics.

--- SENTENCE 10851 ---
With a lack of living material in the eastern Pacific it may never be known for certain if the Panama and Indonesian corals are the same species.

!

--- SENTENCE 10852 ---
*Millepora boschmai* distribution from IUCN copied from http://www.iucnredlist.org.

#### **Habitat**

**Habitat:** *Millepora* species are generally found in inshore areas characterized by turbidity, and exhibit a tolerance for siltation.

--- SENTENCE 10853 ---
*Millepora boschmai* in Panama were found in clear to moderately-sedimented bays protected from high surge.

--- SENTENCE 10854 ---
**Depth range**: *Millepora boschmai* was reported from the upper forereef slope (2 m) to deep, sand and rubble slopes (18 m); however, it was most abundant at the reef base (5–6 m) and deeper outer slope to 12–15 m (de Weerdt and Glynn, 1991).

--- SENTENCE 10855 ---
No known deep refugia.

--- SENTENCE 10856 ---
#### **Abundance**

This species was uncommon prior to 1982 and extremely rare between 1983 and 1997.

--- SENTENCE 10857 ---
It has not been found alive since 1998.

--- SENTENCE 10858 ---
According to de Weerdt and Glynn (1991), *Millepora boschmai* was the least abundant of the three *Millepora* species known from the Gulf of Chiriquí.

--- SENTENCE 10859 ---
De Weerdt and Glynn (1991) reported the elimination of *Millepora boschmai* following the 1982/83 El Niño event.

--- SENTENCE 10860 ---
Detailed searches from 1984 through 1990 across the former range revealed only dead colonies (Glynn and Feingold, 1992).

--- SENTENCE 10861 ---
However, in the early 1990s eight live colonies were found in the Gulf of Chiriquí; five colonies at Uva Island (Glynn and Feingold, 1992), and three colonies at the north end of Coiba Island (Anonymous, 1993; Glynn and Colley, 2001; Glynn et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 10862 ---
However, after the 1997/98 ENSO event, all known colonies were dead (Glynn et al., 2001).

--- SENTENCE 10863 ---
Since then, no live colonies have been observed, despite targeted searches throughout the former distribution.

--- SENTENCE 10864 ---
The only species-specific population information available for this species is an estimate of a pre-1982 total population in the 100s (Glynn, 1997).

--- SENTENCE 10865 ---
However, there is evidence that overall coral reef habitat has declined, and this is used as a proxy for population decline for this species.

--- SENTENCE 10866 ---
This species is particularly susceptible to bleaching, disease, and other threats and therefore population decline is based on both the percentage of destroyed reefs and critical reefs that are likely to be destroyed within 20 years (Wilkinson, 2004).

--- SENTENCE 10867 ---
We assume that most, if not all, mature individuals will be removed from a destroyed reef and that on average, the number of individuals on reefs are equal across its range and proportional to the percentage destroyed reefs.

--- SENTENCE 10868 ---
Reef losses throughout the species' range have been estimated over three generations, two in the past and one projected into the future.

--- SENTENCE 10869 ---
(IUCN, 2010).

#### **Life History**

The reproductive characteristics of this species are unknown.

#### **Threats**

**Thermal stress**: *Millepora* are listed as having a severe susceptibility to bleaching (Marshall and Baird, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 10870 ---
This was borne out by the potential extinction during the 1997/98 El Niño.

--- SENTENCE 10871 ---
**Acidification**: While no studies have been published on acidification impacts on this genus, *Millepora boschmai* is common on eastern Pacific reefs and near-reef habitats where the aragonite saturation state is naturally low due to upwelling (Abramovitch-Gottlib et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 10872 ---
This may imply that to some degree, this species can tolerate acidified water but the impact of acidification on growth has not been quantified.

--- SENTENCE 10873 ---
However, in most corals studied, acidification impairs growth (Langdon and Atkinson, 2005; Manzello, 2010) and, in the case of *Acropora palmate*, impairs fertilization and settlement success (Albright et al., 2010) and is likely to contribute to reef destruction in the future (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007; Silverman et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 10874 ---
While ocean acidification has not been demonstrated to cause appreciable declines in coral populations so far, the BRT considers it to be a significant threat to corals by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 10875 ---
**Disease:** Susceptibility and impacts of disease on this species are not known.

--- SENTENCE 10876 ---
However, there is ample evidence that emerging diseases can have devastating regional impacts on individual coral species (e.g., (Aronson and Precht, 2001; Bruckner and Hill, 2009) and there is evidence that these impacts are occurring in more taxa and at a broader geographic scale (Green and Bruckner, 2000; Sutherland et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 10877 ---
**Predation**: Genus not particularly susceptible to predation by crown-of-thorns seastars (*Acanthaster planci*).

--- SENTENCE 10878 ---
**Land-based sources of pollution (LBSP)

--- SENTENCE 10879 ---
**: The effects of LBSP on the genus *Millepora* are largely unknown.

--- SENTENCE 10880 ---
LBSPrelated stresses often act in concert rather than individually, and are influenced by other biological (e.g., herbivory) and hydrological factors.

--- SENTENCE 10881 ---
Excess nutrients can disrupt corals physiologically (Dubinsky and Stambler, 1996; Fabricius, 2005), but community-level effects on corals are often indirect through competition with algae (McCook et al., 2001; Szmant, 2002).

--- SENTENCE 10882 ---
Toxic contaminants are capable of producing coral mortality, as well as disrupting cellular and reproductive processes (Peters et al., 1997).

--- SENTENCE 10883 ---
Hyposaline runoff can lead to bleaching and mortality (Coles and Jokiel, 1992).

--- SENTENCE 10884 ---
Sediment stress is a complicated response; most sediment impacts are negative (Rogers, 1990; Fabricius, 2005) though some corals are sediment-tolerant.

--- SENTENCE 10885 ---
Collectively, LBSP stresses are unlikely to produce extinction at a global scale; however, they may pose significant threats at local scales and reduce the resilience of corals to bleaching (Carilli et al., 2009; Wooldridge, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 10886 ---
**Collection/Trade**: No trade information for this species was listed on the CITES Trade Database, UNEP World Conservation Monitoring Centre (CITES, 2010).

####

--- SENTENCE 10887 ---
Distribution of points to estimate the likelihood that the status of *Millepora boschmai* falls below the Critical Risk Threshold (CRT; the species is of such low abundance, or so spatially fragmented, or at such reduced diversity that extinction is extremely likely) by 2100.

--- SENTENCE 10888 ---
The BRT was not able to identify factors that reduce potential extinction risk (decrease the likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Millepora boschmai*.

--- SENTENCE 10889 ---
Factors that increase the potential extinction risk (higher likelihood of falling below the Critical Risk Threshold) for *Millepora boschmai* include its bleaching susceptibility, its extremely limited distribution, and the fact that, when it is found, it is always extremely rare.

--- SENTENCE 10890 ---
In the discussion of this species, de Weerdt and Glynn (1991) discussed the risk posed to any coral endemic to the eastern Pacific:

>

--- SENTENCE 10891 ---
"Elements of the eastern Pacific reef coral fauna, consisting of several small, geographically isolated populations in a highly varying environment, would seem to be especially vulnerable to extinction (Wiebe et al., 1975;

--- SENTENCE 10892 ---
D'elia et al., 1981; Wolanski and Delesalle, 1995; Leichter et al., 1996; Lewis, 2006; Paytan et al., 2006; Carilli et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 10893 ---
ENSO events, which started about 2.8 million years ago after the rise of the Panama Isthmus (Ferrier-Pagès et al., 2010), and have since then occurred continuously but un-predictably (Glynn, 1990; Ferrier-Pagès et al., 2010), probably contribute to the poor development of eastern Pacific coral reefs (Glynn, 1990).

--- SENTENCE 10894 ---
Range reductions, which affected the hydrocoral *M. platyphylla* and possibly three scleractinian species (Glynn, 1990; Ferrier-Pagès et al., 2010), may therefore have occurred regularly in the eastern Pacific since the onset of said events.

--- SENTENCE 10895 ---
If *M. boschmai* was endemic to the Gulf of Chiriqui prior to its disappearance, recovery of the species seems highly unlikely, but this can only be ascertained in due time.

--- SENTENCE 10896 ---
"

It is very likely that this species is already extirpated from the eastern Pacific, if not extinct, due to its susceptibility to bleaching events.

--- SENTENCE 10897 ---
Surveys around Uva and Coiba Island in Panama's Gulf of Chiriqui within the last two years turned up no living specimens (Glynn pers.

--- SENTENCE 10898 ---
The overall likelihood that *Millepora boschmai* will fall below the Critical Risk Threshold by 2100 was estimated to be in the "very likely" risk category with a mean likelihood of 96% and a standard error (SE) of 5% (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 10899 ---
This SE was calculated by taking the standard deviation of the seven mean voting scores of the BRT members and shows the coherence among the BRT.

--- SENTENCE 10900 ---
The uncertainty of the BRT is reflected in the range of votes of 66%-100% (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 10901 ---
A.3) and the average range of likelihood estimates of the seven BRT voters (14%).
